### How Does the Animal Cause Fare on the Priority Criteria?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/02-how-does-the-animal-cause-fare-on-the-priority-criteria.html

#### 2.1 Introduction

Animal advocates are often criticized for fighting for animals while there are still humans in need of help. However, if our goal is a world with less suffering, it makes no sense to neglect nonhuman animals or to give them less importance. If we do so, we will be neglecting, or giving less importance to, most of the suffering that occurs in the world. In that case, we will not be efficient at reducing suffering: on the contrary, we will probably increase it even further. Thus, it is not animal advocates who need to explain themselves. Those who need to explain themselves are those who focus on humans, since most of the suffering in the world is endured by other animals.

Because of the predominance of speciesism, most people, when they choose to support a cause, opt for human causes. However, if we apply in an unbiased way the widely used criteria for determining a cause’s degree of priority, which we saw in Chapter 1, it seems impossible to avoid the conclusion that the animal cause should be one of our top priorities. To illustrate this point, below we will see how the situation of nonhuman animals fares against these criteria.

#### 2.2 Seriousness of each victim’s situation

The vast majority of nonhuman animals are born either into the system of exploitation or in the wild. In both cases, the norm is for them to have lives full of suffering (in many cases without any positive experience) and a very premature death, usually an extremely painful one. Of course, there are humans who have lives full of suffering, die prematurely, and have very painful deaths. However, humans do not usually endure a fate equivalent to that of animals on factory farms or in the wild.

#### 2.3 Number of victims

Counting the deaths of vertebrates and invertebrates, terrestrial and aquatic, animal exploitation kills between 34 and 54 trillion animals annually[9]. Important: this number refers only to the deaths of animals resulting from their exploitation. It does not include deaths that are an indirect result of human activities or of natural processes.

For comparison, consider that human deaths (adding up all causes, including natural causes) are estimated at 55.3 million annually[10]. The difference between these numbers is so gigantic that it is hard to visualize. For the sake of argument, let us set aside the number of invertebrates killed and count only the number of fish, birds, and mammals killed annually: “only” about 2 trillion[11]. This amount alone means that in animal exploitation around 5.5 billion vertebrates are killed *per day* (compare this number with the world’s human population, which is 8 billion). If we include invertebrates, somewhere between 93 billion and 147 billion animals are killed *per day*.

In addition, literally astronomical numbers of animals living outside direct human control (such as those who live in the wild) have lives full of suffering and die prematurely because of natural processes themselves. There are no precise statistics on this number of victims, but according to some estimates, at any given moment there are between 1 and 10 quintillion sentient animals in the wild[12]. The difference in size compared to the human population is so astronomical that, to visualize it clearly, we have to resort to analogies. For example, if we draw an analogy with the span of a year, the human population would be, at most, 0.25 *seconds* of the year. All the rest (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 57.5 seconds) would be the animals in the wild. It is like taking a sheet of A4 paper and making a dot with a ballpoint pen (the dot would be the human population; all the white space would be the population of animals in the wild).

#### 2.4 There are so many victims that even speciesists would have to prioritize the animal cause

These numbers are so gigantic that, even if much greater weight were given to the good of humans, curiously, we would still have to conclude in favor of prioritizing trying to change the situation of nonhuman animals. Let us see why:

Suppose that suffering of the same magnitude mattered 10 times more if the victims were human. This would mean that, for us to invest the same amount of resources in helping nonhuman animals as we would invest in helping humans, there would have to be 10 times more nonhuman animals suffering the equivalent (or else, equal numbers of humans and nonhumans suffering, but with the nonhumans suffering 10 times more).

Now suppose that the annual number of nonhuman animals in a situation of extreme suffering were much smaller than it really is: imagine it were “only” one trillion individuals. Imagine that the annual number of humans enduring suffering equivalent to that endured by nonhuman animals were much greater than it really is: suppose it were the entire human population (that is, 8 billion individuals). If human suffering mattered 10 times more than the equivalent suffering of nonhuman animals, then the suffering of the 8 billion humans would be multiplied by 10 (that is, it would be equivalent to the suffering of 80 billion nonhuman animals). The suffering of each nonhuman animal, in turn, would be multiplied by 1 (that is, 1 trillion). Even making all these concessions, in this case we would still have to invest 12.5 times more resources to help nonhuman animals.

If we take the real numbers into account, the ratio is astronomically greater. As we have seen, the world’s human population is around 8 billion and that of sentient nonhuman animals is 1 to 10 quintillion[13]. That is, for every human there are somewhere between 126 million and 1.26 billion sentient nonhuman animals. To deny the priority of improving the situation of nonhuman animals, one would have to postulate that human suffering matters at least 126 million times more than the equivalent suffering of nonhuman animals. From an unbiased point of view, there is no justification even for giving slightly greater weight to the good of humans, much less for a discrepancy of this magnitude.

#### 2.5 How many people already care about this issue?

The number of people devoting themselves to each cause and the resources raised are not proportional to the number of victims each cause deals with.

For example, of all donations made in the United States, 97% of the amount raised goes to human causes[14]. The other 3% goes to environmentalist and animal advocacy causes (and it is not known how much of this 3% goes to the animal cause; it is known only that the popularity of the animal cause is much lower than that of the environmentalist cause).

Even among people who usually donate to the animal cause, on average more than two-thirds of their donations go to human causes[15]. Moreover, part of the resources allocated to human causes is used to buy products of animal exploitation, which contributes to increasing the number of animals who suffer and die.

Thus, it is not just that other animals receive less help than humans do: in the vast majority of cases they receive no help at all and, moreover, they are used as if they were things, which normally entails their deaths and a life of extreme suffering.

As we saw in Chapter 1, section 1.7, the more neglected a cause is, the more difference each additional person working on it makes. Thus, if our goal is to make the world less bad efficiently, the fact that the animal cause is widely neglected (despite the enormous number of victims and the seriousness of the victims’ situation) is an additional reason for us to prioritize it.

#### 2.6 Tractability and the amount of benefit that could be produced

One might think that there is nothing that can be done to change the situation of nonhuman animals and that, therefore, the fact that they represent an astronomical number of victims says nothing in terms of priority, if there is nothing we can do to help the

majority of them. But there are many things we can do for nonhuman animals, and our decisions affect a large number of them. Below are some examples.

(1) With regard to exploited animals, it is possible to choose not to consume them, thus reducing the demand for animal products and the number of animals who would be born into a life of suffering.

(2) Still with regard to exploited animals, it is possible to invest in the development, cost reduction, and deployment of substitutes for the use of animals, such as cultivated meat.

(3) It is also possible to call for changes in public attitudes and in legislation with the goal of recognizing animals as sentient beings who should be protected by rights[16].

(4) There are several ways in which wild animals are already being helped, and much more could be researched in this direction. Studies of this kind could contribute a great deal to increasing efficiency in the use of resources to reduce suffering. For example, studies on the impact of each type of land on the birth rates in the species of those animals who tend to have predominantly negative lives or positive ones could be conducted. This could prevent literally astronomical numbers of animals from being born only to experience extreme suffering.

#### 2.7 Conclusion

If the above analysis is correct, the animal cause meets all the priority criteria very well. The predominance of a speciesist mentality is what keeps it from receiving the importance it deserves.

However, two questions remain: (1) The animal cause deals with several problems. Which ones should be prioritized? (2) Are there other topics that meet the priority criteria just as well (or perhaps even better), which even animal advocates usually fail to notice? We will discuss these questions in the next chapter.

For statistics on the exploitation of terrestrial invertebrates, see Schukraft (2019) and Rowe (2020, 2021a, 2021b). On the exploitation of aquatic vertebrates and invertebrates, see Waldhorn; Autric (2023) and Fishcount (2019). On terrestrial vertebrates, see Our World in Data (2018) and Sanders (2018). ### Among the Problems Affecting Animals, Which Are the Most Important?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/03-among-the-problems-affecting-animals-which-are-the-most.html

#### 3.1 Introduction

As a result of speciesism, most people have prioritized human problems and, in doing so, have neglected problems that affect an astronomically greater number of victims. We discussed this point in the previous chapter.

We will now see how the same problem (neglect of situations that affect a vastly greater number of victims) also affects animal advocates. Below are four examples.

#### 3.2 Neglect of animals exploited for food

The following data concern a single country and certain kinds of animals, but they represent well what happens in general.

Of all the terrestrial vertebrates exploited in the US[17]:

- More than 99.7% are killed in animal agriculture.
- 0.2% are killed in laboratories
- 0.07% are killed in the clothing industry
- 0.03% are killed in shelters.
However, the amount of donations is not proportional to the number of animals affected in each situation. In fact, it is almost inversely proportional.

Of all the donations made to the animal cause in the US[18]:

- 66% go to shelters.
- 32% go to groups with mixed activities.
- 0.7% go to organizations focused on animals in laboratories.
- Only 0.8% goes to organizations focused on farmed animals.
#### 3.3 Neglect of the exploitation of aquatic animals and invertebrates

Even when the animals used for consumption are mentioned, the vast majority of the animals used for this purpose are neglected. For example, animal advocates often mention that around 80 billion animals are killed annually for consumption. However, this estimate refers only to the number of deaths of mammals and birds, which leaves out aquatic animals (vertebrates and invertebrates) and terrestrial invertebrates, who are the overwhelming majority of the animals exploited for consumption.

Below are some data on the annual deaths of animals exploited for food. These statistics are given in the short scale, used in Brazil, in which 1 billion corresponds to 10^9, one trillion corresponds to 10^12, and so on.

- Mammals and birds: about 80 billion[19].
- Fish raised in factory farms: between 51 and 167 billion[20].
- Fish caught directly in the sea: between 787 billion and 2.3 trillion[21].
- Aquatic animals used as feed for the fish that humans raise in factory farms for direct consumption: between 462 billion and 1.1 trillion[22].
- Decapods (shrimp, crabs, and lobsters) raised in factory farms: between 255 and 604 billion[23].
- Silkworms killed for silk production: between 420 billion and 1 trillion[24].
- Insects killed for consumption: between 2 and 3.2 trillion[25].
- There are no data on the number of bees killed for honey production, but the population of bees raised for honey production is between 1.4 and 4.8 trillion individuals at any given moment[26].
- Cochineal insects killed in the production of carmine dye: between 4.6 and 21 trillion[27].
- Shrimp caught directly in the sea and killed: around 25 trillion[28].
The sum of these numbers suggests that somewhere between 34 and 54 trillion animals are killed for consumption annually at the global level. This means that the 80 billion usually mentioned by advocates represent only somewhere between 0.1% and 0.2% of the animals killed for consumption. Shrimp, who represent somewhere between 46% and 73% of the animals exploited, are rarely mentioned by advocates and by authors in the field of animal ethics.

This neglect may occur due to various factors. Here are some examples:

- One of them is the possibility that advocates and authors themselves give less consideration to animals such as insects, crustaceans, and fish. This, in turn, may happen for various reasons, such as, for example, the fact that these animals arouse less empathy in humans, the fact that they are smaller, the fact that they have lesser cognitive capacities, and so on.
- Another is the bias of *scope insensitivity* (also called *scope neglect* or *insensitivity to scope*). When we compare two very large quantities, this bias keeps us from perceiving the difference in magnitude between them. So it is possible that even someone who gives equal consideration to all sentient beings neglects the problems that affect a vastly greater number of animals simply because they do not realize how much greater that number is.
#### 3.4 Neglect of animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes

The situation of animals in the wild as a result of natural processes is even more neglected. Again, this happens due to various factors. Here are some examples:

- There is widespread ignorance of the fact that natural processes maximize the number of animals who are born only to suffer intensely and die prematurely.
- Because of this ignorance, many people mistakenly think that the number of animals suffering in the wild is smaller than the number of exploited animals. Here you can see a comparison of these numbers.
- There is a prevalent belief that we should limit our attention to the harms that animals suffer as a result of human practices.
- Another very common belief is that, if we let nature take its course, the result will be predominantly positive for animals.
- The belief that intervening in natural processes (as long as it is to help animals) is an arrogant attitude is also common.
- When people think of animals in the wild, they tend to think of animals who are not representative of typical life in the wild[29]. They tend to think of large animals, such as lions, zebras, gazelles, and elephants, and they think of adults of these species. These animals are a tiny minority of the animals in the wild. The vast majority of animals in the wild are small, and the vast majority of the individuals who are born usually die very young.
As a result of these and other beliefs, animal advocates have neglected a problem whose scale of harm is so gigantic that it makes even the numbers of animal exploitation (which, as we have seen, are already gigantic) nearly vanish in comparison. There are no statistics on the number of annual deaths of animals in the wild resulting from natural processes. But, to get an idea of the difference in proportion, we can compare the sizes of the populations at a given moment.

- The total population of sentient animals in the wild at a given moment is, according to some estimates, between 1 and 10 quintillion individuals[30].
- Let us compare this, for example, with the world population, at a given moment, of animals raised as stock to be exploited:
o Terrestrial vertebrates: 24 billion[31]. o Fish: 180 billion[32]. o Shrimp: 230 billion[33].

o The sum of these numbers is 434 billion.

If we draw an analogy with the span of a year, the sum of the populations of exploited animals would represent at most 14 seconds. All the rest of the year (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 46 seconds) would be the animals in the wild. This gives us a rough sense of how large the number of animals in the wild is.

#### 3.5 Neglect of the future

The way our decisions influence the history of the world from now on (and, consequently, how they affect the sentient beings who will exist in the future) is a widely neglected question. People in general (including animal advocates) are usually concerned almost exclusively with the problems of the present. When deciding which strategies to adopt to benefit sentient beings, usually only the impact on the sentient beings alive now (or, at most, those who will live in the near future) is taken into account.

This is due in part to the presence of *temporal bias*, which makes an event receive less importance the further away it is in the future. However, if our goal is to achieve the best for all sentient beings, what will matter to us is the magnitude of the harms, not the time at which they occur. Thus, if this is our goal, when deciding which problems to prioritize and which strategies to adopt, we have to imagine as best we can how the consequences of our choices will affect the future, and choose the course of action that is best over time (and not just best in the present or in the near future)[34].

The number of future sentient beings may turn out to be very vast, whether *diachronically* (because the future may be very long) or *synchronically* (since the population of sentient beings may come to increase greatly at each moment). Thus, the number of sentient beings we will affect in the long term with these decisions exceeds by many orders of magnitude the sentient beings who exist now or who will exist in the near future. For this reason, this topic is of crucial importance[35].

#### 3.6 Conclusion

The four examples above seem sufficient to show that the amount of attention given to each problem has not been proportional to the magnitude of each problem. In fact, it has generally been inversely proportional (that is, the most serious problems have also been the most neglected).

This gives us twofold reasons to focus on these problems. First, simply because they are among the most serious problems. Second, because, since they are highly neglected, this is exactly where we can make the greatest difference.

[25] Rowe (2020b).

[34] For an introduction to this topic, see Animal Ethics (2018).

### The Use of Anthropocentric and Environmentalist Arguments in the Animal Cause

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/04-the-use-of-anthropocentric-and-environmentalist-arguments.html

#### 4.1 The strategy of using anthropocentric or environmentalist arguments

There are many ways of advocating for the moral consideration of all sentient beings. These include not only presenting arguments for rejecting speciesism and other forms of discrimination against sentient beings, but also any other forms of activism that promote this consideration, even if *indirectly*.

One example of an *indirect strategy *is to argue against animal exploitation, but with arguments not centered on consideration for animals. Examples include arguing:

- That animal agriculture has a negative environmental impact.
- That animal products are harmful to human health.
- That consuming animals is not natural for humans.
- That torturing animals is training for torturing humans.
- That the way animal products are made is disgusting.
- That animal experimentation poses risks to humans.
- That animal agriculture is related to human hunger.
- That a plant-based diet was the original way of eating of certain peoples.
...and so on.

This strategy is based on two premises:

- The first is the belief that the consequences for animals are the same whether people stop exploiting them out of consideration for them or for other reasons (“for animals, what matters is what you do, not what you think”).
- The second is the belief that these anthropocentric or environmentalist arguments are more efficient at leading people not to exploit animals because, since people are speciesist, they would be more easily convinced by them.
In this text, we will discuss this strategy[36].

#### 4.2 Some problems with the use of anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments

There are at least two ways in which the two premises above can be questioned:

- It is not only the exploitation of animals that matters. Also mattering are the harms suffered by animals in the wild as a result of natural processes[37] and the new forms of suffering that may arise in the future[38]. As we will see in the next section, anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments, besides not addressing these problems, may increase them.
- Contrary to what may initially seem to be the case, the different motivations for ceasing to exploit animals do not have the same consequences.
Both points will be explained in more detail in the next section.

#### 4.3 Why different motivations have different consequences

In planning a strategy, we need to take into account all the likely consequences we can estimate, and not just some of them. Thus, we have to take into account not only the direct impact of the use of animal products but also, crucially, the impact of the worldview we strengthen with each strategy.

The influence each person has through their consumption lasts until the end of their life. The effects of the worldview they pass on, by contrast, extend over centuries or millennia, since they affect how other people will decide and how they will influence still other people to decide. The values people adopt guide the way they make all their decisions throughout their lives, and they also determine which values they pass on to other people, including future generations. In short, there is a snowball effect.

With this in view, we have reasons to think that arguments centered on consideration for animals would have a better impact, especially in the long term, since they help increase moral consideration for sentient beings, something no other argument does. In fact, as we will see in the following sections, the use of arguments not centered on consideration for animals could even increase the harms to sentient beings.

#### 4.4 Do indirect arguments make it easier to accept considering sentient beings?

It could be objected that speciesism is often defended not because people believe it is correct, but as an excuse, simply because they like the taste of animal products. Thus, in defense of using anthropocentric or environmentalist arguments, it could be said that, if people stop consuming animals, for whatever reason, it will be easier for them to accept an antispeciesist view later on.

The same would hold for other forms of animal exploitation, such as animal experimentation. According to this view, the people who defend it do not do so because they consider it just, but simply because they do not want to give up the benefits they have obtained from it (for example, having built scientific careers performing experiments on animals).

Therefore, according to this view, getting people, by whatever means, to stop exploiting animals may be more efficient for achieving a world in which sentient beings receive full consideration than advocating for that consideration itself.

This argument is based on an idea that seems correct. However, if the argument succeeds, the conclusion that follows is that we should combine this strategy with advocacy of consideration for sentient beings. Why? Because the argument only indicates that lines of argument not centered on consideration for animals would help with consideration for sentient beings. But that consideration would still be necessary to prevent harms in the long term. Thus, even if the argument were correct, the use of arguments not centered on animals would at most facilitate the expansion of moral consideration for animals. However, if this is so, then it makes sense to think that, to achieve it, it is probably more efficient to spread it directly than to spread other ideas.

Moreover, it is possible that people who defend animal exploitation do so simply because they give very little consideration to nonhuman animals (and not because they consider exploitation wrong and defend it simply to disguise the fact that they do not want to give up consuming animal products). If they considered animals even a little, the enormous amount of suffering and death caused by animal exploitation should already be a minimal motivating reason for them to try to give up, or at least reduce, their consumption of animals. Now, if this does not happen, and if these people would give up consuming animals for anthropocentric or environmentalist reasons, this is a sign that they strongly believe in anthropocentric and environmentalist values. So it is at the very least uncertain whether their stopping consuming animals for anthropocentric or environmentalist reasons would make it easier for them to later accept considering all sentient beings.

#### 4.5 Risks of using arguments not centered on consideration for sentient beings

*The risk of implying that animals do not matter *

There is also the risk that the use of anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments may delay (or even prevent) consideration for sentient beings. For example, if even when the subject is the exploitation of animals the arguments used to address the issue have nothing to do with the harm to animals, this may help emphasize that the suffering and death of animals is something that does not matter much (or even that does not matter at all). Thus, the use of arguments not centered on consideration for animals may help strengthen the speciesist view, which is precisely the cause of the terrible situation in which animals find themselves.

*The risk of strengthening views opposed to consideration for animals *

Since anthropocentrism and environmentalism involve values diametrically opposed to consideration for sentient beings, using arguments grounded in these values carries a great risk of making it harder to accept sentience-centered values.

*The risk of increasing animal exploitation *

Another possible effect of using indirect arguments is to convey the idea that, if animals are being harmed without negatively affecting humans or the environment, then that is fine. This may help encourage the search for more sustainable ways of exploiting animals that may be even worse for them, such as confining them in even smaller spaces, or promoting the consumption of aquatic animals and insects, which would cause a vastly greater number of animals to die, since these animals are much smaller. These practices may even be beneficial for humans or from an environmentalist point of view.

In these cases, the use of arguments not centered on animals may help considerably increase the number of exploited animals, resulting in more animals being killed than even if nothing had been said against animal exploitation.

*The risk of increasing the suffering of wild animals *

The use of anthropocentric and environmentalist arguments may also contribute to neglect of the suffering of wild animals resulting from natural processes and to a rejection of the proposal to help them[39]. Besides possibly leading people to approve of forms of animal exploitation that are sustainable or advantageous to humans, it may also lead people to advocate practices such as the expansion of natural territory[40], space colonization[41], and disregard for possible future nonorganic sentient beings[42]. All these risks, if realized, would generate much more suffering than animal exploitation[43].

#### 4.6 Conclusion

One of the main reasons why there are risks that suffering of astronomical magnitude will be generated in the future is the fact that those who could affect sentient beings positively or negatively do not give them moral consideration. Thus, to reduce such risks, it is essential not to postpone advocating for the moral consideration of all sentient beings.

[37] For more on this topic, see Cunha (2022) and Animal Ethics (2023 [2020]).

[39] One study suggests that people who stop consuming animal products for environmentalist reasons become more resistant to the proposal of helping animals in the wild. See Greig (2017).

[42] On this risk, see Mannino *et al.* (2015); Tomasik (2015b); Baumann (2022, p. 12-3, 82-3).

### The Total Approach and the Sufficient Approach

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/05-the-total-approach-and-the-sufficient-approach.html

#### 5.1 Introduction

In this chapter we will look at two possible approaches to trying to get more people to accept the goal of pursuing a better world for all sentient beings: the *total approach* and the *sufficient approach*. We will see some advantages and disadvantages of each of these approaches, and it will be argued that it is more promising to combine them, at least in most contexts. Several examples will also be presented of particular contexts in which they can be applied and combined, and of how this could be done.

#### 5.2 Ranges of compatibility: open and closed

What we will call the *range of compatibility* concerns the number of additional ideas that need to be accepted in order to accept a given idea. The more additional ideas are needed, the more *closed* the range will be, since fewer people accept those additional ideas together. The fewer additional ideas are needed, the more *open* the range will be, since in that case it is more likely that more people will accept the idea, whatever they think about other questions.

It is important to identify how wide an idea’s range of compatibility is, because if we think an idea has a more closed range when in fact it has a more open one, we will miss the opportunity to get many more people to accept it. This is illustrated by the following example.

Suppose we want to defend idea A, and we believe that, to accept it, one must also accept idea B. We then start defending B in order to get people to accept A. In doing so, we imply to the public that, to accept A, one has to accept B. Imagine that we manage to convince some people to accept A, but that other people do not accept it precisely because they do not accept B. But imagine that we later discover that, to accept A, it was not necessary to accept B. Then we could have convinced many more people to accept A if we had not defended B (or, at least, if we had not implied that, to accept A, it was necessary to accept B).

Thus, if, for people to accept an idea A, it is not necessary for them to agree about other ideas B, C, D, E, and so on, then it is better to emphasize that, whatever they think about these other ideas, they can still accept A.

Emphasizing that, even if there is disagreement about other things, there could still be agreement about what we are proposing has at least two advantages. The first, an obvious one, is that it increases the likelihood that a much larger and more diverse number of people will accept what we are proposing. The second is that it tends to reduce polarization[44], since it emphasizes that, despite the many disagreements, there may be some goals in common.

#### 5.3 Examples of views compatible with multiple views in ethics and politics

To accept the following goals, it is not necessary to adopt a specific view, whether in terms of ethical theory or in terms of political orientation:

- Consideration for all sentient beings.
- Rejection of speciesism.
- Abolition of animal exploitation.
- Veganism
- Reduction of the suffering of wild animals.
- Prevention of risks of future suffering.
- Concern for the long-term future.
- Consideration for nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist in the future.
Thus, instead of defending a specific view in ethics or politics and pointing out that one implication of that view is accepting those goals, we are more likely to get people to accept these goals if we argue that they should be accepted by everyone, regardless of which view in ethics or politics they adopt. Defending specific positions may give the mistaken impression that, to accept the goals in question, it is necessary to accept those specific views (with the result that those who do not accept such views reject these goals).

#### 5.4 The total approach and the sufficient approach

Above we gave examples of goals that can be accepted in their entirety by various positions. At other times, however, depending on what someone thinks about other questions, they will accept a given goal only to a certain extent.

When we argue in favor of an idea, we usually understand the situation in terms of accepting it or rejecting it entirely. However, there is the possibility that someone might accept it partially. Of course, if we defend a given idea, we will think it best that other people accept it fully. However, it can be well worth emphasizing that certain arguments that are sometimes put forward in an attempt to reject the idea we are proposing do not actually imply rejecting it, but rather accepting it partially. By emphasizing this, we increase the chances that even those who disagree with its complete acceptance will still accept it at least to some extent.

In this sense, we can distinguish two approaches:

*Total approach:* defending what we believe to be the best decision.

*Sufficient approach*: emphasizing that even those who disagree with our position can accept it partially or accept some of its implications.

**Important:** these are not mutually exclusive strategies. In fact, at the end of this chapter it will be argued not only that we have better chances of better results if we combine both, but also that it is risky to employ only one of them.

The following table lists several examples of these approaches with regard to various topics:

| **Topic ** | **Total approach ** | **Risks involved ** | **Sufficient approach ** |
| Criterion for moral consideration | Arguing that the beings we ought to consider are sentient beings, and only sentient beings. | Those who think we owe moral consideration to nonsentient entities may think they are justified in disregarding sentient beings. | Emphasizing that even those who argue for considering nonsentient entities should recognize that being sentient should be *sufficient *for being considered, and that there are still reasons to prioritize sentient beings over nonsentient entities, whether these are wholes or living organisms. |
| Ethical theory | Defending a specific ethical theory that we consider most plausible, and showing that it implies rejecting speciesism. | Those who do not accept that specific theory may think they do not need to reject speciesism. | Emphasizing that, to accept the arguments for rejecting speciesism, it is not necessary to adopt a specific ethical theory. |
| Political orientation | Defending a specific political orientation, and showing that its ideals are realized only if we reject speciesism. | Those of any other political orientation may think they do not need to reject speciesism. | Emphasizing that speciesism should be rejected, regardless of which political orientation someone prefers. |
| Veganism | Advocating veganism. | Given the prevailing degree of speciesism, many people may find the standard too demanding and not change their consumption at all. | Emphasizing that even those who have not yet become vegan can still reduce their consumption and do other things to help animals. |

| Speciesism | Rejecting speciesism and arguing that we ought to give equal consideration to all sentient beings. | Given the prevailing degree of speciesism, many people may not agree with this and therefore think they need not give any consideration at all to nonhuman animals. | Emphasizing that, even if humans deserved greater consideration, this would not imply that animals deserve no consideration at all, nor that they deserve little consideration. |
| Speciesism and cause prioritization | Arguing that equal consideration implies prioritizing the situation of nonhuman sentient beings (given the number of victims, degree of neglectedness, etc.). | Speciesist people, because they disagree with equal consideration, may think they need not pay much attention to the situation of nonhuman animals. | Emphasizing that, even if someone gives greater weight to humans, given the number of victims, they would still have to prioritize the situation of nonhuman animals. It also helps to emphasize that, even if someone prioritizes human problems, they should still consider it very important to do something for nonhuman animals. |
| Magnitude of the harm of death | Arguing that belonging to the human species or having greater cognitive capacities does not necessarily imply being harmed by death to a greater degree. | People who disagree with this may think that animals are harmed little by death. | Pointing out that, from the fact that one individual is harmed by death to a greater degree than another, it does not follow that the individual who is harmed less is harmed little by death. |

| The harm of death | Arguing that nonhuman animals are harmed by death. | Those who think they are not harmed by death may think it is justified to exploit them or not to help them when they are victims of natural processes. | Showing that, in the vast majority of cases, for us to be against their exploitation and in favor of helping them in the wild, it is enough to recognize that they are harmed by suffering. |
| Well-being of sentient beings | Defending a specific position in the theory of well-being. (For example, arguing that all that matters, in terms of the well-being of sentient beings, is suffering and pleasure — that is, defending a hedonistic theory of well-being). | People who believe that other things matter in themselves for well-being (preference satisfaction, knowledge, relationships, etc.) may think that suffering and pleasure do not matter. | Emphasizing that believing that things other than suffering and pleasure matter for well-being does not imply that suffering and pleasure do not matter. |
| Prioritization with regard to the future | Arguing that we should prioritize the long-term future and prioritize avoiding risks of future suffering (called s-risks). | Those who disagree with this may think they need not be concerned with the long-term future and with s-risks. | Emphasizing that even those who have other priorities still have reasons to think that the long-term future and avoiding s-risks are very important. |

| Interventions affecting wild animals: sentience-centered goals versus environmentalist goals. | Arguing that, when making decisions that affect wild animals, we should adopt a view centered solely on sentience (and reject environmentalist goals), and that this implies helping animals in the wild. | People who adopt environmentalist values may think they are justified in opposing helping wild animals | Pointing out that arguing that nonsentient entities are morally considerable does not show that sentient beings are not, and that we still have reasons to prioritize sentient beings, even if we had to consider nonsentient entities. It can also be shown that many programs to help wild animals do not conflict with environmentalist goals (some would even help achieve them). |
| Focus on the situation of animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes (compared to exploited animals). | Arguing for focusing on the situation of animals in the wild who are victims of natural processes, rather than on exploited animals (given the number of victims, degree of neglectedness, tractability, etc.). | People who focus on exploited animals may think they are justified in disregarding the situation of wild animals. | Emphasizing that even those who have other focuses should still devote at least part of their activism to talking about the issue of wild animal suffering. |

| Moral responsibility for natural harms and anthropogenic harms | Arguing that we have as much moral responsibility for natural harms as we have for anthropogenic harms. | People who believe they are more responsible for anthropogenic harms may think we have no duty to do anything about natural harms | Emphasizing that arguing that we are morally responsible to a greater degree for one thing does not imply arguing that we are not responsible for another (one can argue, for example, that we are responsible to a high degree, even if to a lesser one). It can also be emphasized that the amount of natural harm is so much greater than that of anthropogenic harm that we would still have to prioritize reducing natural harms even if we gave much greater weight to anthropogenic ones. |
| Helping wild animals and veganism | Arguing that we ought to be vegan and also be in favor of helping animals in the wild. | Those who are not vegan may think they can be in favor of helping wild animals only if they someday become vegan | Emphasizing that, if we can do something to help, we should do it, regardless of whether or not we are doing other things to help. |
| Activism strategies | Emphatically defending certain activism strategies that we believe to be the best. | Advocates who prefer other strategies may think that mutual commitments with us are not possible. | Emphasizing that we can agree on certain strategies even if we disagree on others. It also helps to emphasize that, despite the strategic disagreement, the goal pursued is shared. |

| Consideration for sentient beings and other philosophical questions | Defending consideration for sentient beings and also speaking out openly on various other philosophical questions (ethical, political, metaphysical, epistemological, etc.) | The range of disagreement on all these questions is very wide. This may lead people (especially if we defend controversial views on other topics) not to accept our advocacy of consideration for sentient beings. | Emphasizing that consideration for sentient beings can be accepted regardless of what someone thinks about other philosophical questions. However, this does not mean that we should not take sides on these other questions, even if they are highly controversial (although that is another possibility as well). |
| Criteria for sentience and the nature of consciousness | Defending a specific position in philosophy of mind about the nature of consciousness and arguing that it implies recognizing that beings with a centralized nervous system are sentient. | People who do not accept this specific position in philosophy of mind may think they are justified in denying that beings with a centralized nervous system are sentient | Arguing that we should recognize that there is a correlation between brain states and mental states, whatever we think consciousness is (for example, regardless of whether we hold a substance dualist, property dualist, physicalist monist, or idealist monist position, etc.) |

| Controversial implications of what we defend | Openly stating that what we defend has some controversial implications, and arguing that it is common sense that is wrong. | People may not accept our proposal if they realize it has these controversial implications. | Emphasizing that, even if someone disagrees about what to do in the controversial cases, this does not imply rejecting the proposal as a whole. For example, someone’s rejecting interventions in conflicts between animals does not imply rejecting vaccinations, treatment of diseases, disaster relief, etc. Another option is to hide the controversial implication. However, if the public notices the implication on its own, it will consider us dishonest for hiding it. |

#### 5.5 Conclusion: it is important to combine both strategies

As we have seen above, both strategies, if used in isolation, carry risks. The risk of the total strategy is that people will mistakenly understand that, if they do not fully accept a certain view, they have no reason to partially accept what is being proposed. The general risk of the sufficient strategy, in turn, is that it does not discuss questions that are in fact very important and about which people perhaps ought to change their minds.

Thus, the question is about the degree of focus we should have on each strategy, since it seems better to use both. For example, one option is to focus on the total approach and emphasize that even those who do not agree could still partially accept what has been defended. Even if we opt for a greater focus on what is sufficient, this does not mean that arguing in favor of the total goal is not important. For example, a world in which many people are antispeciesist certainly has very different consequences from a world in which many people merely consider nonhuman animals, but to a lesser degree. Thus, the total approach is also very important (at least in many of the contexts listed above).

The decision to focus more on the total or on the sufficient approach depends on knowing what would achieve our goals most efficiently. For example, would they be better achieved if a larger number of people accepted them partially or if a smaller number of people accepted them completely? The answer to this will depend, in the case of each goal: (1) on the number of people who would accept it fully versus the number of people who would accept it partially; and (2) on how much more each person who accepts it fully would do to achieve the goal, compared with those who accept it partially.

Regardless of the answers to these difficult questions, it seems that arguing only in favor of the ideal, without emphasizing what is sufficient, involves high risks. On the other hand, talking only about what is sufficient means not daring to discuss very important controversial questions. Starting to discuss these questions as soon as possible can make a difference in the long term, by making the public less averse to thinking about them.

**Notes**

[44] On why polarization increases the risks of suffering, see Baumann (2022, ch. 9).

### Shifting the Focus in Debates: Why Is Speciesism Rarely Discussed?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/06-shifting-the-focus-in-debates-why-is-speciesism-rarely.html

#### 6.1 Shifting the focus

It is not uncommon, in debates about practices that harm nonhuman animals, for the defenders of such practices to try to keep the focus of the discussion on aspects that have nothing to do with the harm to animals. Below are some examples.

- If the subject is the use of animals for consumption, they will approach the topic as if what mattered for knowing whether or not such practices are justifiable were the risks to human health and the environmental impacts. They will then argue that consuming animals can indeed be healthy and sustainable.
- If the subject is animal experimentation, they will approach the topic as if what mattered for knowing whether such practices are justified were the benefits to humans. They will then argue that animal experimentation can indeed be safe for humans.
- If the subject is the killing of wild animals motivated by environmentalist ideals, they will treat the question as if what mattered for knowing whether or not such practices are justified were whether or not they help achieve environmentalist goals. They will then argue that such killing is justified because the animals belong to invasive species and pose a threat to native flora and fauna (for example, because they feed on rare plants or interbreed with native animals and produce hybrids, so that the native species is no longer “pure”), and so on.
In none of these cases is it discussed whether, even if such claims are true, these practices might still be unjustifiable because of the harm they cause to animals. Our obligations toward animals and speciesism are rarely discussed topics. It is not that these people go so far as to argue that we should not have consideration for animals, or that this consideration should be very small. The question is simply ignored completely. It is as if it did not exist.

Sometimes this is planned. For example, someone may realize that they have no good arguments to justify speciesist practices, but, since they do not intend to change their position, they shift the focus so that it does not become clear that they have no good arguments.

In other cases, however, such a shift may happen without being premeditated. Some of these people may not even have any idea that the way our decisions affect animals is an ethical question. They may find it so obvious that animals do not deserve respect that it does not even cross their minds that this idea might be mistaken.

Whether or not it is planned, the fact is that in most debates the focus ends up being shifted, and the moral consideration of animals is not discussed. As pointed out below, this result also comes about largely because of the collaboration (again, intentional or not) of the people who say they are there to defend animals.

#### 6.2 Falling into the trap

Animal advocates’ response to the shift of focus is usually, curiously, to accept it and start discussing the other questions raised by those who seek to justify the practices that harm animals. Surprisingly, animal advocates themselves rarely discuss the moral consideration of animals (and the shift of focus often comes from animal advocates themselves!). Below are examples in the three contexts listed above

- *Example 1*. Defenders of consuming animals claim that it is justifiable because it can be healthy and sustainable. Animal advocates could simply reply that, even if that is the case, consuming animals would still be unjustifiable, just as killing humans in order to consume them would be unjustifiable even if it were healthy and sustainable.
Animal advocates could ask the following: “why would one act be right because it is healthy and sustainable, while another act would be wrong despite being equally healthy and sustainable?” Defenders of consuming animals would probably answer that it is because in one case the victims are human and in the other they are not. And animal advocates could ask why species would be a morally relevant criterion rather than an arbitrary criterion, as race and gender are, and so the debate would continue.

However, that is not what usually happens. Animal advocates usually focus on contesting the claim that consuming animals can be healthy or sustainable.

- *Example 2*. Defenders of animal experimentation claim that it is justified because it can offer benefits to humans. Again, here animal advocates could reply that the fact that a practice offers benefits to members of one group does not automatically justify that practice, especially when the harms to members of other groups are being counted in an arbitrary way (in this case, the harms to animals receive less weight, or receive no weight at all).
An analogy could be drawn with the human case. If a scientist claimed that it is justified to perform experiments on dark-skinned humans because this would benefit light-skinned humans, it would be very clear that pointing this out is insufficient to justify such a practice. One could then ask the following: “why would one practice be right because it produces benefits, despite the harms it causes, while another would be wrong because of the harms it causes, despite producing benefits?”

Again, defenders of experimentation would probably say that the difference is that in one case the victims are human, and in the other they are not. But, again, animal advocates could ask why species would not be an arbitrary criterion like skin color, and so the debate would continue.

But that is not what happens. Animal advocates usually limit themselves to arguing that animal experimentation, due to differences in physiology, is not safe for humans.

- *Example 3*. Defenders of the killing of wild animals motivated by environmentalist ideals claim that it is justified because these animals pose a threat to environmentalist ideals. Again, here one could reply that this seems insufficient to justify the killing. After all, there is no species that poses a greater threat to environmentalist ideals than the human species, yet this does not seem to justify killing humans en masse.
So one could ask the following: “why would one killing be right because it protects environmentalist ideals, while another would be wrong despite protecting environmentalist ideals (to a greater degree)?”

Again, defenders of the killing would say that it is because in one case the victims are human and in the other they are not. And, again, one could question the criterion of species, and so the debate could proceed.

But, again, that is not what animal advocates usually do. They choose to argue that killing animals is not good from an environmentalist point of view.

In short, animal advocates could contain the shift of focus and bring the focus back to the discussion of the moral consideration of animals. But that is not what they usually do. They usually “buy into” the shift of focus. The result is that the moral consideration of animals is rarely discussed. Why does this happen? That is what we will discuss in the next section.

#### 6.3 Why do animal advocates accept the shift of focus?

Just as the shift of focus by those who defend practices that harm animals may or may not be planned, the acceptance of the shift by animal advocates may or may not be conscious.

Below are several hypotheses about why animal advocates accept the shift. Of course, these hypotheses are not the only possibilities. And, more importantly, these hypotheses are not mutually exclusive, since the motivation may differ in the case of different people and even in the case of the same person in different situations.

Hypotheses:

*1) Distraction. *

Animal advocates may not notice that the focus is being shifted. When they do notice (if they notice at all), they are already tangled in the web, discussing other questions, without knowing how to bring the focus of the debate back to the moral consideration of animals.

*2) Embarrassment *

Animal advocates may notice that the shift of focus is taking place, and disagree with it, but be embarrassed to really defend animals. There is a considerable likelihood that this happens in many cases because of how great an influence social pressure exerts. Since society is highly speciesist, it is quite possible that some people do not defend animals out of fear of being ridiculed (this is compounded if they do not know arguments to defend their position).

*3) Agreement *

It is also possible that, although they present themselves as animal advocates, some of these people are not in fact advocates, and agree that the harms to animals are not decisive for knowing whether or not the practices in question are justified, and for this reason they accept the shift of focus.

For example, there are many people who call themselves vegan but who do not mean by this that they seek to avoid harming animals as much as possible and that they are against their exploitation, but rather that they do not consume animal products for environmentalist or health reasons, or out of concern for disadvantaged human beings (even though this is not what the term veganism means). Again, the change in the meaning of the concept of veganism may be intentional (to make the public think that these people are there to defend animals) or due to ignorance, because they have no idea what veganism is.

*4) The belief that it is not possible to discuss ethics *

Another possibility is that some people accept the shift of focus because they believe that it is not possible to discuss ethics. For this reason, they limit themselves to discussing factual claims.

The belief that “in ethics, everything is relative/subjective” and that there are no views that are more or less plausible is quite common. So someone who holds this belief might think: “these people believe it is justified to disregard animals and I disagree, end of story, there is nothing to discuss.”

According to this view, it is not possible to assess whether the goals someone pursues are right or wrong, just or unjust: all that could be done is to investigate whether or not a given action leads to the goal pursued.

Thus, if an animal advocate thinks this way, and realizes that, for the people they are talking to, all that matters is humans or environmentalist goals, they will try to show that consuming animals is not healthy or sustainable, that animal experimentation poses risks to humans, that the killing of wild animals does not achieve environmentalist goals, and so on. In short, the belief is that it is impossible for someone to come to consider animals because it is impossible for someone to change their position regarding goals, values, principles, and so on.

It is surprising that such people think this way. After all, the overwhelming majority of people who are animal advocates today were not always so. For example, the vast majority used to consume animals and at some point in their lives stopped to reflect and concluded that there was no justification for doing so. So it is strange that they believe both that there is nothing to reflect on in this regard and that it is not possible for people to change what they think about it.

Moreover, anyone who knows a little about animal ethics knows that attempts to justify speciesism have been widely discussed at least since the 1970s. When we look at this debate, it becomes very clear how problematic the attempts to justify speciesism are and how solid the arguments in favor of the equal consideration of all sentient beings are. The idea that in ethics all positions are equally plausible sounds reasonable only if we do not take the trouble to look at the arguments offered by each side.

Indeed, if a person has no good argument to defend their position and their opponent has a good argument to defend the opposite position, it is always a good excuse to claim that all positions are equally plausible and that there is no right and wrong.

*5) The belief that it is possible to discuss ethics, but impossible to change people *

Another possibility is that some animal advocates agree that it is possible to discuss ethics, and that it is even possible to show that speciesism is unjustifiable, but believe that it is impossible for people to change what they think, even when they know they are wrong. According to this view, “some are born good, others are born bad, period.” However, once again, animal advocates should know from their own case that things are not like this.

*6) The belief that it is more efficient to limit oneself to discussing the facts *

Finally, another possible motivation for animal advocates to accept the shift of focus would be that, although they recognize that there are strong arguments against speciesism and that it is possible to change what people think, they believe that not questioning speciesism (and limiting themselves to discussing the factual claims made by the defenders of speciesist practices) is more efficient for convincing the people they are talking to to stop harming animals.

For example, animal advocates might think that, since they do not have to question the goals and values their opponents adopt, it is easier to get them to change their attitude if they manage to show that the practice in question does not fit with their goals and values.

One problem with this strategy is that very often the goals and values of their opponents will be better achieved by harming animals. For example, it is true that there are many forms of animal consumption that are not healthy and whose ways of exploiting animals are not environmentally sustainable. However, there are various other forms that are (and it is always possible to try to create others that are). Animal experimentation to benefit humans poses risks to humans because of physiological differences. However, animal experimentation to benefit animals of the same species does not pose this risk. Similarly, there are cases in which the most efficient way to secure environmentalist goals is not to harm wild animals (or even to help them). However, at other times the most efficient way to achieve environmentalist goals is to harm animals.

What happens in many cases is that animal advocates insist that it is not possible to exploit animals sustainably, that food of animal origin can never be healthy, and so on. That is, they need to “stretch” the facts to make them fit what they want to defend. But this should not be the path; rather, we should not be afraid to present arguments against speciesism. We will look at something on this below:

When the discussion is limited to the facts, speciesism is never questioned. Speciesism is the reason animals are in the situation they are in. Therefore, it seems impossible to change this situation without questioning speciesism. Moreover, when someone accepts the shift of focus, they are, even if unintentionally, reinforcing the anthropocentric and environmentalist views and emphasizing that animals really do not matter in themselves (and this has a great effect on the public, especially as people notice that animal advocates simply say nothing in favor of animals). So it is not just that accepting the shift of focus may be ineffective at changing the situation of animals: it has a good chance of being counterproductive.

Finally, there is a strategic problem with this view. If we aim to be as efficient as possible at changing people’s behavior in ways that favor animals, then it is better to focus on the audience that shows greater openness to considering animals, since that way it is more likely that their values will come to be aligned with the goal of favoring animals (and we will then achieve a better result by focusing on these people). It seems that many animal advocates have the impression that it is impossible to change people’s behavior in ways that favor animals because they have chosen to focus precisely on the audience most averse to thinking about the moral consideration of animals.

#### 6.4 Conclusion

We have seen in this chapter that, in debates about practices that harm animals, the focus is usually shifted to questions that have nothing to do with the harm to animals. This shift of focus ends up implying that the harm to animals is not decisive (or even important) for knowing whether or not such practices are justifiable.

We have seen that this shift of focus, depending on the case, may or may not be intentional on the part of those who try to justify the practices that harm animals. We have also seen that, likewise, the acceptance of the shift of focus by animal advocates may or may not be deliberate. However, we have seen that, regardless of whether or not it is deliberate, the shift of focus has the same effect: speciesism is not discussed.

There are no good reasons for animal advocates to accept this shift of focus because, as long as speciesism is not widely discussed, there will be no change in the way people see nonhuman animals and, as a consequence, the situation of nonhuman animals will hardly change, since the root of the problem will then never be attacked.

### Moral Beliefs, Motivation to Act, and the Role of Ethical Reflection

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/07-moral-beliefs-motivation-to-act-and-the-role-of-ethical.html

#### 7.1 The case of animal ethics experts who consume animals

This chapter is intended as a brief reflection on the question of moral motivation, based on cases that sometimes come up in the debate on the moral consideration of nonhuman animals.

Animal ethics is the area of applied ethics that studies the morality of our decisions that affect nonhuman animals. It is sometimes argued that the fact that there are animal ethics experts who continue consuming animals is proof that believing that something is right/wrong has no influence whatsoever on changing people’s attitudes.

According to this view, for people to care about changing a practice, it is not enough for them to conclude that it is wrong: something is needed that “touches” them, such as a shocking image or video, a song, an event in their personal lives, reading a moving story, and so on. In short, according to this view, nonrational persuasion is always necessary.

In this text it will be argued that it is hasty to conclude, from the fact that there are animal ethics experts who consume animals, that the belief that something is right/wrong therefore does not create a motivation to act accordingly. As we will see in the following sections, there are at least five other possibilities that may be occurring in the case of these experts.

#### 7.2 Perhaps they do not consider consuming animals wrong

One possibility is that some of these people are experts in animal ethics but, for some reason, do not agree that consuming animals is unjustified. If this is the case, these people are doing exactly what they believe to be right. Of course, this does not mean that they *are* right to think so. It only means that, if this is what is happening, then pointing to the case of these people does not show that the belief that something is right/wrong does not influence attitudes (quite the contrary: it is their belief that consuming animals is justified that makes them continue to consume animals).

#### 7.3 Perhaps they consider consuming animals only slightly wrong

There are degrees to which people consider an action right or wrong. For example, we normally consider running over a pedestrian a very serious wrong. On the other hand, arriving fifteen minutes late to a meeting is normally considered a minor wrong. That is why we take much more care not to run someone over than to avoid arriving late to a meeting. If this is so, then *how much* someone thinks a practice is right or wrong has a great deal of influence on how much they will strive to act accordingly.

Thus, it is possible that some of these experts give some moral consideration to nonhuman animals, but much less than that given to humans. Thus, even if they say they consider consuming animals wrong, perhaps they do not consider it a particularly serious wrong. And, once again, the case of these people does not support the thesis that someone’s beliefs about what is right and wrong have no influence on their attitudes. Quite the contrary: if this is what is happening, it shows that their attitude reflects precisely their belief that animal exploitation is not a very serious wrong.

#### 7.4 Perhaps they are not being sincere about what they report

It could be objected that there are people who say they consider the use of animals for consumption extremely wrong, yet do not stop consuming them either. However, this is still not enough to conclude that the belief that a practice is right/wrong does not motivate someone to act accordingly. This is so for two reasons, explained below.

The first is that someone may say they consider consuming animals extremely wrong but not be sincere and, in fact, not consider it all that wrong. The second is that, even if they are being sincere, such a person may display the problem known as *weakness of will*, which we will address in the next section.

#### 7.5 Perhaps they have a weak will

It could be claimed that there are people who sincerely consider consuming animals an extremely serious wrong and yet do not stop consuming animals. That is, these people display the problem known as *weakness of will*.

However, although cases of weakness of will show that moral beliefs do not *by themselves* determine someone’s behavior, they do not show that moral beliefs have no *influence* on behavior. In the case of these people, the motivation generated by the belief that consuming animals is an extremely serious wrong probably has to compete with other, opposing motivations (for example, social pressure, the pleasure obtained from foods they are already used to, the emotional association between food of animal origin and social events, and so on).

#### 7.6 Perhaps they decide not to do what they feel motivated to do

Yet another possibility is that the moral belief creates a motivation to act accordingly, that there are no other conflicting motivations, but that the person simply decides not to do what they consider right and feel motivated to do. Such cases seem to be rarer. But, again, such cases would show only that moral beliefs do not *determine* someone’s behavior; they would not show that moral beliefs do not create a *motivation* to act accordingly.

#### 7.7 Conclusion

The fact that there are animal ethics experts who consume animals is not enough to conclude that someone’s beliefs about what is right/wrong to do do not generate a motivation to act accordingly. As we have seen, there are at least five other possibilities for what is happening in these cases: (1) they do not consider consuming animals wrong; (2) they consider consuming animals wrong, but not seriously wrong; (3) they say they consider consuming animals seriously wrong, but they are lying; (4) they consider it seriously wrong, but the motivation generated by this belief has to compete with other, opposing motivations; (5) they consider it seriously wrong and there are no opposing motivations, but they decide not to do what they feel motivated to do.

All this may cause some people to feel disappointed about the power of arguments to change people’s behavior. However, this is hasty. What we have seen above shows only that arguments are not magical tools that give us control over the decisions of those who will hear the arguments. As we have seen, a person’s behavior is the result of many factors and, however well someone argues, and even if the other person accepts the argument, we have no power to decide whether or not they will follow in practice what they have concluded. Only they can do that.

In view of this, some people might then think that it is better to abandon rational persuasion and adopt tactics of nonrational persuasion. But the point is this: any other form of persuasion has the same limits. Faced with tactics of nonrational persuasion, a person may simply pay no attention, or may say they agree and not act accordingly (again, there may be conflicting motivations, they may simply decide not to follow what they feel motivated to do, and so on). Indeed, tactics of nonrational persuasion seem to have even greater limits, since rational persuasion at least manages to explain the reasons for accepting or rejecting a given practice. This seems to show that rational persuasion, with all its limits, is still the best we have.

### Normative Objections Disguised as Strategic Objections

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/08-normative-objections-disguised-as-strategic-objections.html

#### 8.1 Normative objections and strategic objections

Sometimes someone does not agree with a given goal. We will call this a *normative objection*. At other times, someone agrees with the goal but believes that a given strategy will not be efficient for achieving it. We will call this a *strategic objection*.

Sometimes people sincerely report whether their objection is normative or strategic. However, there are cases in which someone says their disagreement is strategic, but in fact does not agree with the proposed goal. In this text we will explore how this happens in debates on questions of animal ethics.

#### 8.2 The claim that “this would be great, but it won’t work”

There are many cases in which someone states that they agree with a certain proposal but claims that defending it would be futile (that is, that it would have no effect) or even counterproductive (that is, that it would have the opposite of the intended effect).

Arguments of this kind frequently arise against any position that points out that we should be concerned with something that until then we had not seen as a problem. Below we will look at some examples.

#### 8.3 Examples in questions of animal ethics

Below are examples of arguments of this kind in seven different contexts:

**Example 1. **Faced with the proposal to give moral consideration to animals, saying something like:

*“I agree that we should consider animals. However, if it is already hard for people to consider humans, let alone other animals. So it is better to leave the defense of animals to future generations and for now defend only humans, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to come to consider animals. Pointing out now that the reasons for considering humans imply considering animals will only make people find the very idea of moral consideration absurd and then refuse to consider even humans.” *

**Example 2: **Faced with the proposal to fight speciesism, saying something like:

*“I agree that we should reject speciesism. However, if it is already hard for people to reject racism and sexism, let alone speciesism. So it is better to leave the fight against speciesism to future generations and for now focus only on fighting racism and sexism, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to reject speciesism. Pointing out at the present moment that rejecting racism and sexism implies rejecting speciesism will only make people reject neither racism nor sexism.”*

**Example 3: **Faced with the proposal to advocate the abolition of animal exploitation, saying something like:

*“I agree that animal exploitation should be abolished. However, if it is already hard for people to accept exploiting animals less, let alone accept abolishing exploitation. So it is better to leave the advocacy of abolition to future generations and for now focus only on reforms of animal exploitation, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept abolishing it. Advocating abolition now will only make people reject even reducing the suffering of exploited animals.”*

**Example 4: **Faced with the proposal to draw attention to the situation of invertebrates (since they are the vast majority of animals, both in the system of exploitation and in the wild), saying something like:

*“I agree that we should consider invertebrates. However, if it is already hard for people to consider vertebrates, let alone invertebrates. So it is better to leave the defense of invertebrates to future generations and for now focus only on vertebrates, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to consider invertebrates. Defending invertebrates now will only make people refuse to consider even vertebrates.”*

**Example 5: **Faced with the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes saying something like:

*“I agree with the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural processes. However, if it is already hard for people to accept being vegan, let alone accept caring about suffering and death that do not result from human practices. So it is better to leave this question to future generations and for now focus only on veganism, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept the proposal to help wild animals. Pointing out now that considering animals implies, besides rejecting their exploitation, also helping wild animals will only make people fail to reject even exploitation.”*

**Example 6: **Faced with the proposal that we should do something to prevent suffering from being multiplied to astronomical levels in the future, saying something like:

*“I agree with concern for the long-term future. However, if it is already hard for people to care about the present or the short term, let alone the long term. So it is better to leave the advocacy of concern for the long term to future generations and for now focus only on the present or the short term, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept concern for the long term. Pointing out now that **considering the sentient beings of the present or the near future * *implies considering the sentient beings of the distant future** will only make people refuse to consider even the sentient beings of the present.*

**Example 7: **Faced with the proposal that, if nonorganic sentient beings come to exist in the future, they should receive as much consideration as any other sentient being, saying something like:

*“I agree with consideration for nonorganic sentient beings. However, if it is already hard for people to accept considering animals, let alone accept considering nonorganic sentient beings. So it is better to leave the defense of all sentient beings, organic and nonorganic, to future generations and for now focus only on animals, since that is what will make it possible for people in the future to accept considering nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist. Pointing out now that considering animals implies considering nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist, will only make people refuse to consider even animals. *

The examples above are just a few samples of this type of argument. As should now be clear, they all follow the same pattern (which we will detail in section 8.7), and this pattern appears in many other contexts. However, the examples above are sufficient for what this text aims to discuss.

#### 8.4 One possibility: the real motivation is not the one stated

Something common to all the examples above is that the objections are presented as strategic objections. That is, the person raising the objection emphasizes that they agree with the proposed goal, but claims that defending it (or at least defending it now) will be futile or even counterproductive.

It is possible that, in several of the cases in which the above claims are made, the reservation really is strategic. However, there is at least one other possibility: the person does not in fact agree with the proposed goal, but says they are against defending it for strategic reasons.

In short, it may be that, although what is said is “don’t do this because it won’t work,” the real fear is exactly the opposite: “don’t do this because it might work, and I don’t want that result.” That is, although what is said is “there’s no point in defending this because no one will accept it,” it may be that the real fear is that people will accept what is being proposed. In these cases, what is sought is to get the other person to give up defending an idea one disagrees with, while pretending to agree with it.
