### The Debate on Cultivated Meat

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v8/12-the-debate-on-cultivated-meat.html

#### 12.1 Introduction

In this chapter we will first look at what cultivated meat technology is and then address three debates about this technology. The first debate discusses the objections put forward by those who defend conventional meat. The second, the objections put forward by animal advocates. Finally, the third discusses the advantages and disadvantages of cultivated meat compared to other strategies for changing the situation of animals.

#### 12.2 What cultivated meat is

Cultivated meat is also known as cell-based meat, synthetic meat, in vitro meat, clean meat, artificial meat, or lab-grown meat. It is meat obtained by culturing animal cells. The cells are generally obtained by biopsy from animals and are then cultured, resulting in structures similar to the muscle tissues found in animal meat[73]. In the final stage, the process involves shaping, seasoning, and coloring, and the result is a final product with the same appearance, flavor, and texture as conventional meat[74].

The production of cultivated meat usually involves extracting cells from a nonhuman animal (living or dead) by means of a tissue biopsy[75]. The cells of interest are then isolated and placed in a bioreactor, where they are expanded to create a greater cell yield, and are afterward placed on a scaffold to mature into a specific form[76]. To expand the cells in the bioreactor, a cell culture medium with a nutrient-rich solution is used. In some cases this solution contains fetal bovine serum (FBS), produced from blood drawn from a dead cow fetus. However, the cultivated meat industry is moving from FBS to plant-based serums[77].

The main cells used are skeletal muscle myocytes, adipocytes (fat cells), and fibroblasts (connective tissue)[78]. The samples include differentiated cells and stem cells. Both types are primary cells and exhibit limited proliferation once removed, unlike what happens in immortalized cell lines (which, owing to a chance or induced mutation, evade the natural mechanisms of cellular senescence and can keep dividing practically indefinitely[79]).

Embryonic stem cells, being pluripotent, are a good option for the cultivated meat process[80]. But since they are difficult to obtain and to differentiate efficiently into the desired cell lines, a more viable alternative is adult stem cells, since they are found in a variety of tissues, although they have a more limited capacity for differentiation[81].

Cultivated meat is not limited to the production of beef. There is already considerable work on cultivated meat from birds[82], pigs[83], fish[84], decapod crustaceans such as shrimp and lobsters[85], and even for the production of dairy products[86]. In theory, it is possible to produce cultivated meat from any animal, including humans[87].

#### 12.3 Potential for acceptance/rejection of cultivated meat

Cultivated meat is already available for human consumption in Singapore, the US, and Israel, and has been approved in the United Kingdom as food for animals such as dogs and cats[88].

The cultivated meat industry has the potential to grow enormously. For example, one survey found that 70% of the UK population is willing to buy cultivated

meat[89]. Another example is the fact that large conventional meat companies, such as Cargill and Tyson, have invested heavily in cultivated meat[90].

However, cultivated meat also faces rejection. For example, in November 2023 Italy banned cultivated meat outright, preventing it from being developed or sold in the country[91].

#### 12.4 Discussing the main objections to cultivated meat

The great advantage of cultivated meat technology, in terms of avoiding harm to animals, is that it provides a product practically identical to conventional meat, but (depending on the method) without the need to kill animals or subject them to the extremes of suffering to which they are typically subjected when they are exploited for food.

However, cultivated meat also faces objections. In the next sections we will discuss some of the most frequent ones. In sections 5 to 8 we will discuss objections that are not focused on concern for animals. In sections 9 to 14 we will discuss objections focused on concern for animals.

#### 12.5 The objection that it is not natural

A first objection to cultivated meat accuses it of not being natural. This objection is usually raised in defense of conventional meat. This was, for example, one of the central reasons for the ban on cultivated meat in Italy.

A first possible reply to this objection is to maintain that cultivated meat is in fact natural, since it is made of cells just like conventional meat. Moreover, it is obtained by growing cells, without involving any genetic modification of them. However, one could respond that what is meant when it is claimed that cultivated meat is not natural is that it goes through several procedures before resulting in the final product, and all of these procedures involve the use of technology. Yet to this one could reply that

conventional meat likewise goes through a series of procedures that also involve the use of technology.

A second way of replying (the correct way, in my view) is to point out that, even if cultivated meat is not natural and conventional meat is, this does not imply that we should reject cultivated meat, nor that conventional meat is justified. After all, just as the fact that something is natural does not imply that it is necessarily good[92], the fact that something is not natural does not imply that it is necessarily bad. For example, suppose it were shown that conventional meat is natural and cultivated meat is not. If bringing about less suffering and fewer deaths in the world is more important than obtaining a natural product, we will in that case have to reject the natural product.

At this point some people might claim that obtaining a natural product is more important than avoiding suffering and deaths. However, this position is very likely speciesist or, at the very least, selfish. For example, if humans were being bred and killed for their meat, and we ourselves had to face that fate, no one would object to cultivated meat on the grounds that it is not natural. This shows that the position holding that obtaining a natural product is more important than avoiding suffering and deaths fails the impartiality test and therefore cannot be just[93].

#### 12.6 The objection that it would pose risks to consumers

Another objection claims that the problem with cell-based meat is that it could have unforeseen negative effects on those who consume it. For example, Wrenn (2024, p.8) claims that animal protein is toxic to humans and that the normalization of in vitro meat will worsen serious diet-related public health crises, disproportionately harming vulnerable human communities that lack the resources and infrastructure to cope with them[94]. The author (2024, p.8) concludes that "vegans should not promote toxic products, especially when healthier and more accessible alternatives are available," referring to plant-based food.

There are at least two possible replies to this objection, discussed below.

The first reply involves noting that cultivated meat is intended as an alternative to conventional meat, not to the consumption of plants. Thus, to assess the claim that its normalization will worsen serious public health crises, what has to be compared is not a scenario in which x number of people consume cultivated meat with a scenario in which they would eat only plants, but rather a scenario in which x number of people consume cultivated meat with a scenario in which they would consume conventional meat.

Cultivated meat is no less safe for consumers' health than conventional meat. In fact, it is much safer, since cultivated meat facilities have a high degree of control over the environment, so the chances of contamination with pathogens such as salmonella and E. coli are quite limited[95]. Although it is always possible for cultivated meat to be contaminated in other ways (as happens with any food, including plants), this risk is many times smaller than it is in the case of conventional meat[96].

Moreover, since cultivated meat production does not house live animals and hygiene standards are high, it could do a great deal to reduce the frequency of zoonotic disease outbreaks[97] and also to reduce antibiotic resistance[98]. If left unchecked, antibiotic resistance threatens to make simple infections fatal once again[99]. The main driver of antibiotic resistance is animal agriculture, owing to the enormous quantity of antibiotics routinely administered to exploited animals[100]. Although cultivated meat also uses antibiotics to reduce the risk of contamination, research in the field suggests that in the future antibiotics will no longer be routinely used in cultivated meat production[101].

The second reply, in turn, points out that, even if cultivated meat were less safe for consumers than conventional meat, the risk consumers would run does not come anywhere close to the harms animals endure when they are exploited.

For example, conventional meat results in a gigantic number of animal deaths, and results in most of them having lives full of suffering. Moreover, this harm is certain (and not merely a risk), and the animals are forced into that fate. On the other side, even if every person who consumed cultivated meat suffered some kind of harm, the number of victims would still be vastly smaller than the number of victims of animal exploitation, and the harm per victim would still be vastly smaller than the harm to each exploited animal (at least compared to the suffering to which animals exploited in factory farming are subjected). Moreover, in the case of consumers, this would be a risk (and not a certain harm, as it is for the animals), and a risk they would choose to run of their own accord, since they are not obliged to consume it (they can, for example, eat only plant-based food), unlike the animals.

In short, the fact that a practice involves a risk, or even an actual harm to humans, does not imply that we have conclusive reasons to reject it. The risks and harms to everyone affected (including nonhuman animals) in each of the available courses of action would have to be weighed in an unbiased way. We saw above that cultivated meat is probably safer than conventional meat. But even if it were less safe, once we take into account the harms to each of the affected parties (human and nonhuman), comparing conventional meat and cultivated meat, the balance would still tip in favor of cultivated meat.

#### 12.7 The objection that it is not yet sustainable

Another objection accuses cultivated meat of not being a sustainable technology, since it would use far more resources to produce the equivalent amount of food compared to the production of plant foods. We will now discuss three possible replies to this objection.

The first reply points out that, since cultivated meat is a very recent technology, it is likely that, if more resources are invested in it, over time it will become increasingly cheap to produce, perhaps even to the point of coming to use fewer resources in the future to produce the equivalent amount of food, even compared to the production of plant foods. It is uncertain whether this would actually happen. But it is something we could only know if the same amount of resources were invested in both forms of food production over the same period of time.

The second reply, in turn, points out that cultivated meat aims to be an alternative to conventional meat (not an alternative to a plant-based diet), and that, even if it makes sense to say that growing plants is more sustainable than cultivated meat, it does not make sense to say that conventional meat is more sustainable than cultivated meat.

For example, compared to conventional meat, cultivated meat facilities require much less land and water and are responsible for fewer greenhouse gas emissions[102], requiring 64% to 90% less land and causing 20% to 94% less air pollution[103].

Finally, the third reply points out that, to know whether we should invest in technology A or B, it is not enough to know which of the two is more sustainable: what we need to know is which of them is better taking into account all the sentient beings affected. Thus, even if cultivated meat were less sustainable than conventional meat, the fact that cultivated meat avoids the death and suffering of trillions of individuals would show that it would still be preferable to conventional meat, even if it were less sustainable.

#### 12.8 The objection that it harms the most vulnerable humans

Another objection to cultivated meat is the claim that it harms disadvantaged humans because of the technology's potential to be exploited for profit in capitalist societies.

For example, Wrenn (2024, p.8) opposes cultivated meat, claiming that "the effort to globalize diets rich in animal protein is rooted in colonialism, racism, and classism," and argues (referring to plant-based food) that "healthier and more

accessible alternatives are available and already existed before Western capitalism began privatizing land and undermining traditional food production around the world"[104]. The author concludes that, because of this, "in vitro meat may be palatable to venture capitalists, but it is unlikely to create meaningful social change for nonhuman animals"[105].

A first possible reply to this objection is to point out that capitalists will seek to maximize their profits in any case, and so it is preferable that they do so using cultivated meat rather than conventional meat, since this would greatly reduce the amount of suffering and death caused to animals. Therefore, it is not true that cultivated meat would not create meaningful change for nonhuman animals. In fact, the changes would probably be extremely significant.

This also shows that it is false that cultivated meat would increase the inequality resulting from capitalism (since companies would seek to maximize profits in any case, whether with cultivated meat, with conventional meat, or with plant production). The difference would be that cultivated meat would result in a world with less total suffering and fewer total deaths compared to a world with conventional meat.

A second reply is to point out that, even if cultivated meat increased the inequality resulting from capitalism, it does not follow that there would be conclusive reasons to reject it. The fact that it has the potential to considerably reduce the total amount of suffering and death of nonhuman animals would have to be taken into account. Weighing the harms and benefits to everyone affected, it would still have a far more positive balance than conventional meat, even if it increased inequality among humans.

An objection to this reply would be to say that, in that case, what we should advocate is a plant-based diet, since it would involve even less suffering and death than cultivated meat. Again, this could be answered in two ways, discussed below.

The first is to point out that, if cultivated meat comes to be developed, perhaps in the future it will involve less animal suffering and death than even growing plants, since plant production also causes suffering and death to a large number of small animals who live in the fields (through the use of pesticides, harvesting methods, etc.).

The second reply is to point out that it is very unlikely that animal exploiters would agree to switch to plant production, but it is quite likely that they would switch to cultivated meat if it turns out to be more profitable than conventional meat. Thus, if a campaign against cultivated meat were successful, the result would not be animal exploiters switching to plant production, but rather maintaining the production of conventional meat. Therefore, there is no reason for animal advocates to be against cultivated meat, even if they believe there are better options than it.

#### 12.9 The objection that the producers do not care about animals

Some people oppose cultivated meat on the grounds that it is produced by large companies that are driven by profit and do not care about animals[106].

A first possible reply to this objection is to point out that the people who own cultivated meat companies, who work at such companies, or who invest in them are, in their vast majority, vegans or vegetarians[107].

A second reply is to point out that whether cultivated meat companies care about helping animals is irrelevant: what is relevant is the impact on animals[108]. For example, Bryant (2024, p. 10) argues that we should prefer a company that does not care about animals but reduces harm to animals over a company that cares about animals but lacks the capacity to do anything about it[109].

#### 12.10 The objection that cultivated meat does not solve every problem

Cultivated meat is sometimes rejected on the grounds that it "is not a panacea for the horrors of animal use and exploitation[110]," since it "will not benefit animals raised for the production of dairy, eggs, wool, leather, experimentation, or entertainment"[111].

A first possible reply to this objection is to point out that, if cultivated meat technology comes to be developed, it may also come to replace these other products or practices that currently use animals. For example, as we have seen, there are already dairy companies that use cultivated meat technology[112].

A second reply is to point out that what needs to be assessed is not whether cultivated meat solves all the problems of animals, but whether it is efficient at solving the problem it sets out to solve. After all, other initiatives that benefit animals, such as alternatives to the use of animals in science, the adoption of abandoned animals, and attempts to ban specific practices of exploitation, are not rejected because they do not solve the problems of all animals. If the fact that a form of activism does not cover every problem affecting animals meant that we should reject it, then veganism or any other form of activism focused on exploited animals would also have to be rejected, since they do not address the issue of animals who suffer in the wild as a result of natural processes[113] or the problems related to the future[114], for example.

#### 12.11 The objection that the impact may be smaller than expected

Another objection to cultivated meat points out that there is currently no certainty about whether it might one day grow to the point of largely replacing conventional meat and actually leading to far fewer animals being used in the food system[115].

It is true that there is no such certainty. However, this is not enough for us to conclude that it is not worth investing in this technology. What would have to be assessed is whether the potential benefit

justifies the investment, and whether or not there is some other, more promising form of investment, in terms of benefiting animals, in which the same resources could be invested. Pointing out that there is no certainty about whether it might one day come to largely replace conventional meat does not answer these questions, not least because whether or not this will actually happen depends on how much is invested in cultivated meat, compared to investment in conventional meat.

Moreover, the investment that large conventional meat companies make in cultivated meat has already been growing. Thus, if animal advocates campaign against cultivated meat, the most they can achieve is that these companies invest in conventional meat the resources they could have invested in cultivated meat, and the result will then be that cultivated meat will not come to replace conventional meat.

#### 12.12 The objection that cultivated meat is still of animal origin

Some animal advocates object to cultivated meat on the grounds that, since it is a product made with animal cells, it would not be a vegan product.

One reply to this objection is to point out that the concept of veganism concerns avoiding harm to animals, and so what matters is knowing the impact cultivated meat will have on animals. For example, suppose that cell-based meat did not harm animals in any way. In that case, given the definition of veganism as the practice of avoiding harm to animals, cell-based meat would be vegan (even if it were made with animal cells).

However, it could be objected that the adjective vegan cannot be applied to a food of animal origin, even if it did not harm animals in any way. Yet in that case one could reply that whether or not the food is vegan then does not matter for knowing whether we should support it or reject it: what matters is knowing its impact on animals.

Accordingly, it seems crucial to know whether cultivated meat harms animals in any way and, if so, whether that harm is sufficient for us to reject it, or whether its potential benefit to animals could outweigh that harm. That is what we will discuss next.

#### 12.13 The objection that cultivated meat still harms animals

One of the main objections of animal advocates to cultivated meat is the fact that, at least at present, it requires taking cells from animals, and therefore some animals would have to be kept as a source of cells[116].

Moreover, it is also pointed out that most of the existing literature on the subject, whether in academic publications or on the websites of cultivated meat companies, does not describe what happens to the animals during the cell extraction procedure, nor what happens to the animal after the biopsy[117]. Some authors claim that, presumably, they share the same fate as most other farmed animals, that is, they are killed[118]. However, there are companies that state that the animals they use are not killed[119].

An advocate of cultivated meat could reply by pointing out that, even if this is a harm to these animals, it does not come anywhere close to the harm they would endure with conventional meat, where, besides being killed, they would probably have a life full of intense suffering. It would still be true that cultivated meat could radically reduce the number of animals who suffer and die in animal agriculture[120].

To this, the opponent of cultivated meat could reply that we should reject both conventional meat and cultivated meat because both use animals as resources. According to this reply, what we should do is advocate veganism. For example, the Vegan Society's policy on cultivated meat states the following:

“As it currently stands, the cultivated meat process is not sufficient for us to support it. [...] There is already a plethora of vegan meat alternatives that are not derived from cultivated or lab-grown meats[121].

In short, what proponents of this argument mean is that showing that cultivated meat is better than conventional meat is not enough to justify it, since there is an even better option: veganism.

The advocate of cultivated meat could reply to this in two ways. The first would be to point out that at present it is necessary to use animals to obtain the cells, but perhaps in the future some procedure will make it possible to obtain cells indefinitely, such as the use of immortalized cell lines or cloning, for example.

The second reply points out that there is no realistic possibility of persuading animal exploiters to switch to producing plant-based food (since the demand for meat would continue), but there is a realistic possibility that, if cultivated meat technology turns out to be more profitable for them, they will switch to cultivated meat.

Accordingly, the advocate of cultivated meat could point out that, if someone is going to cause harm, it is obviously preferable that they cause a lesser harm. Since in this case conventional meat would cause an overwhelmingly greater harm, it is important to advocate cultivated meat. Thus, the advocate of cultivated meat could accuse its opponents of not knowing how to deal with *trade- offs* (losses and gains). The result of someone refusing to advocate cultivated meat on the grounds that it would still cause some harm to animals would probably be that animals continue to be exploited in the worst possible ways, since animal exploiters have an extremely low probability of adopting veganism but a good probability of adopting cultivated meat production if it turns out to be more profitable for them.

At this point some opponents of cultivated meat argue that they bear no responsibility whatsoever for what will happen, since that will depend on the exploiters' decisions, not theirs. However, if we can influence someone's decision, it seems that we are at least partially responsible for what will happen, whether we decide to exert influence or decide not to. For example, let us imagine that, left to himself, an animal exploiter will adopt neither cultivated meat nor veganism. Let us imagine, however, that the probability of our persuading him to stop using animals is very low, but that the probability of our persuading him to adopt cultivated meat is high. If we decide not to influence him to adopt cultivated meat, then the probability that he will continue to exploit animals as much as he already does is very high. This outcome is, at least in part, our responsibility, since we play a crucial role in how the outcomes unfold.

However, the opponent of cultivated meat could point out that, in real life, we are not in a position to influence each animal exploiter as the example suggests. Yet the advocate of cultivated meat could reply that it is the very fact of whether or not the technology is available, and how economical it is, that will be the decisive factor of influence, since if cultivated meat becomes cheaper than conventional meat, the exploiters themselves will prefer to use it, and that we can play a role in this process by advocating the importance of developing cultivated meat.

To this the opponent of cultivated meat could reply that, if the exploiters themselves are going to adopt it anyway should it become cheaper to produce than conventional meat, then there is no need for animal advocates to support it. However, the advocate of cultivated meat could reply that, if animal advocates' support for cultivated meat helps accelerate its development, cost reduction, and implementation, then they should provide that support, if their goal is really to benefit animals.

On the other hand, if the opponents of cultivated meat succeed, the most they would achieve with their campaign against cultivated meat is to get animal exploiters not to use (or to use fewer) resources on cultivated meat. However, the exploiters would probably not use those resources to create vegan products, but rather to exploit animals to make conventional meat.

The opponent of cultivated meat could deny that their actions have any influence on the exploiters' decisions. One could reply to this, first, that if the movement against cultivated meat grows, there could be social pressure against the technology (as happened in Italy), and the result, again, would be harmful to animals. Second, one could reply that, if the opponent of cultivated meat believed their actions had no influence whatsoever, they would not campaign against cultivated meat.

Furthermore, the advocate of cultivated meat could argue that, if in the future it is sufficiently developed, it may come to cause less harm to animals than even the production of plant-based food. For example, in crop fields a very large number of small animals die as a result of cultivation and harvesting methods. This problem does not exist (or would exist to a much lesser extent) in the case of cultivated meat, since it would be developed in controlled environments. Thus, even if animals came to be used to obtain the cells, this would still have a far smaller negative effect than that resulting from plant production. Moreover, as already mentioned, it may be that in the future it will become unnecessary to use animals to take the cells to produce cultivated meat.

At this point opponents of cultivated meat sometimes argue that, even if growing plants harms animals more than cultivated meat, growing plants is still preferable, because in that case the harm is *collateral*, whereas in the case of cultivated meat the harm is *instrumental* (that is, it is a means to the end).

Again, there are two possible replies here. The first is to point out that the harms to animals resulting from growing plants are often not collateral. For example, in crop fields, the deaths of animals resulting from the use of pesticides are an instrumental harm, since the use of pesticides is a means to the end of growing plants.

However, let us suppose that all the harms resulting from growing plants were collateral. The second, more important reply points out that whether the harm is collateral or instrumental is an agent-centered concern, not a concern for those affected by the decision. In other words, if what really matters to us is avoiding harm to animals as much as possible, we will base ourselves on determining which course of action has the best harm/benefit ratio for the animals affected, and not on whether the harm is collateral or instrumental (since, for the animals affected, this makes no difference whatsoever). This reveals that activists who repudiate instrumental harms but do not care about avoiding collateral harms (in this case, greater than the instrumental harms) are concerned with feeling falsely pure, not really concerned with the animals.

#### 12.14 The objection that cultivated meat reinforces speciesism

An objection sometimes raised against cultivated meat is the accusation that it reinforces speciesism and may, for that reason, be counterproductive in terms of changing the situation of animals.

For example, Wrenn (2024, p. 8) argues that "it is important to recognize the symbolic violence that cultivated meat sustains"[122]. She compares cultivated meat to encouraging white supremacists to amuse themselves with AI-generated simulations of slavery, and to encouraging teenagers to take pleasure in school-shooting video games as an alternative to real violence[123]. She argues that, just as these symbolic acts of violence can have negative consequences for humans, cultivated meat may further fuel the normality of speciesism and meat consumption and have negative consequences for animals[124].

According to the author, cultivated meat will become the next “happy meat,” with producers employing tactics similar to those they currently use to block public knowledge of how animals are harmed during production[125].

She argues that, on the other hand, plant products that convincingly imitate the taste and texture of animal meat do not threaten to reinforce speciesism to the same extent that cultivated meat could, since in that case consumers are aware that these analogues are of plant origin[126].

Criticisms of this kind rightly point out that cultivated meat is not free from the risk of causing harm (indeed, no practice is). However, this by itself is not enough to conclude that we should reject it. What would have to be compared are the probable harms/benefits resulting from a scenario in which resources would be invested in cultivated meat with other scenarios in which those same resources would be invested in other things (in addition to trying to imagine where those resources would probably be invested if they were not invested in cultivated meat).

It is possible that, if the same resources were invested in antispeciesist outreach, the results for animals would be better than if they were invested in cultivated meat (although this is also quite uncertain). However, it must be borne in mind that, while vegan investors would have some probability of investing in antispeciesist outreach if

they did not invest in cultivated meat, the probability that the animal exploiters who invest in cultivated meat would do so is extremely low, perhaps zero. Accordingly, we should encourage at least animal exploiters to invest in cultivated meat since, otherwise, they would invest those resources in exploiting animals. This does not mean that cultivated meat is free from causing harm to animals. It means only that the scenario that would probably occur in its absence would involve a vastly greater amount of harm, besides lacking the benefits it would bring.

The harms and benefits that would probably result need to be weighed taking into account the current state of the world. For example, since at present human slavery and school killings are not the everyday norm, it may be that encouraging the creation of virtual simulations of slavery and school killings has the potential to cause more harm than good. However, in a scenario in which human slavery and school killings were the everyday norm, if creating virtual simulations of these practices would considerably reduce their real occurrence, then doing so would have a positive balance, even if it also had the potential to cause some harm.

Moreover, it is also possible to question the thesis that cultivated meat would reinforce speciesism. For example, Bryant (2024, p. 9) argues that cultivated meat is likely in fact to help reduce speciesism, because speciesist attitudes both cause and are caused by the consumption of animals, since defenses of speciesism are often motivated by the desire to keep eating meat[127]. Thus, if people stop eating animals, it may be easier for them to accept rejecting speciesism.

#### 12.15 Advantages and disadvantages of focusing on changes in food technology

There is great polarization among animal activists regarding cultivated meat. There are both activists who strongly repudiate it and activists who see it as the definitive solution to the problems affecting nonhuman animals. As we have seen, both stances are completely mistaken. Polarization leads people to tend to see things in "all-or-nothing" terms, which is completely removed from reality. Seeking to avoid this, below we will try to list both some advantages and some disadvantages of

focusing on cultivated meat compared to other activist strategies for benefiting animals. This will provide a more realistic picture of the situation.

The debate about focusing on cultivated meat is an example of a more general debate about strategies focused on technological change versus strategies focused on social change[128]. Thus, several of the things said here about the specific case of cultivated meat also apply to other technologies.

Important: in this and other similar debates, what is under discussion is not necessarily "should we focus on this or that strategy?" (although that is also a possibility). Another possibility is: *how much* should we focus on this or that strategy? Additional questions are: (1) is it better for everyone to have the same degree of focus on certain strategies, or is it better for different people to focus on different strategies? (2) Is it better for the same person to have the same degree of focus on certain strategies all the time, or is it better to vary the degree of that focus, and what does this depend on? We will not discuss these questions here for reasons of space, but it is important to remember that they are important questions if our goal is to be efficient in our activism.

Regardless of the answers to these questions, it is always possible to try to list the advantages and disadvantages of each strategy, its reach and its limitations. That is what we will try to do below with the question of cultivated meat.

In the following list, although some points are clearly strengths and others clearly limitations, there are others that are strengths/limitations at present but may cease to be so in the future, or that are strengths/limitations depending on whether or not the focus on cultivated meat is accompanied by other activist strategies. For this reason, the points in the following list are not classified as strengths or as limitations.

Points to take into account when assessing the degree of focus on cultivated meat:

(1) The greater the consumption of cultivated meat compared to conventional meat, the more animals are spared suffering and being killed.

(2) Cultivated meat has the potential to produce behavioral changes in agents who are indifferent to the fate of animals. That is, cultivated meat can lead even people who do not care about animals to stop consuming them

(3) If developed, cultivated meat technology may also come to replace eggs, milk, and dairy products on a large scale, benefiting an even greater number of animals.

(4) Perhaps cultivated meat technology or similar technologies may in the future also come to be used as an alternative method to animal experimentation and to xenotransplantation. For example, closely related technologies are tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, both developed from human cells[129].

(5) If cultivated meat becomes more profitable for the exploiters, they themselves will want to abandon the use of animals.

(6) For cultivated meat actually to replace the use of animals on a large scale, it is not enough for it to give advantages to the exploiters: it must also give advantages to the public. This is because the public will not necessarily be receptive to cultivated meat. For example, some people may raise the banner of "that's not natural!" or spread rumors that it is dangerous, and so on. However, if the public sees advantages in cultivated meat, the probability of acceptance is much greater. An example of an advantage for the public would be its becoming cheaper and/or tastier than conventional meat.

We can draw a parallel with the gradual replacement of animal traction owing to the emergence of the automobile. One of the key factors in this replacement was the fact that the automobile offered the public many advantages compared to horse-drawn carriages (speed, comfort, protection, etc.).

(7) Note that, as happened in the case of animal traction, the existence of a substitute, even one offering advantages to the public, does not guarantee that animal exploitation in that area will end. Today there is less use of animal traction, but animals still continue to be exploited for this purpose. Likewise, it is likely that, if cultivated meat comes to be cheaper to produce and offers advantages to the public, its large-scale implementation will happen and this will greatly reduce the number of exploited animals, but this alone does not guarantee that animal exploitation for consumption will end. Therefore, it is necessary to combine technology-focused activism with activism focused on changes in consideration for animals.

Moreover, since the adoption of cultivated meat does not, by itself, change people's mindset regarding speciesism, it does not prevent setbacks in what is done to animals. For example, if people remain speciesist and some more profitable way of exploiting animals emerges in the future, they would probably go back to exploiting animals. Thus, activism focused on technologies that replace the use of animals is not a substitute for antispeciesist activism. Indeed, it needs such activism so that there are no setbacks.

On the other hand, however, the adoption of cultivated meat may make social change easier in terms of the rejection of speciesism. Many people defend speciesism not because they believe it is correct, but simply because they like the taste of animal products. Thus, if in the future people do not have to give up that taste because they are already consuming cultivated meat, it may be easier for them to accept an antispeciesist worldview. Therefore, the adoption of cultivated meat may also have the potential to facilitate the rejection of speciesism. However, there is also the possibility that many people defend speciesism simply because they think it is correct, and not because they like the taste of animal-based food. Yet in this case, too, the only way to combat such a view is by setting out the arguments against speciesism. So, either way, antispeciesist activism is always necessary.

(8) At present, the focus of activism centered on cultivated meat has been almost exclusively on reducing the number of exploited animals. However, the technology also seems to have the potential to be applied to reduce the suffering and deaths that animals endure as a result of natural processes[130]. Incredible as it may seem at first glance, the number of animals who suffer and die as a result of such processes (hunger, thirst, disease, natural disasters, conflicts between animals, etc.) is vastly greater than the number of exploited animals. Cultivated meat technology could be used, for example, to reduce the incidence of predation[131]. Just as cultivated meat is already available for dogs and cats in certain places, it could become available in the future for wild animals, and this could be applied both to predators under human control (for example, in sanctuaries) and to those in the wild.

#### 12.16 Conclusion

Above, we saw what cultivated meat technology consists of and addressed three debates surrounding it.

The first debate addressed objections to cultivated meat that are not centered on concern for animals. We saw that all of these objections suffer from speciesism and would not pass the impartiality test, and are therefore unjust.

The second debate addressed objections to cultivated meat put forward by animal advocates. We saw that, although at present cultivated meat still involves the use of animals as a source of cells, this may be unnecessary in the future. We also saw that, even if cultivated meat still causes some harm to animals, if animal exploiters do not invest in cultivated meat, they will very probably invest those resources in practices that result in far more harm to animals (and to a far greater number of animals). Moreover, we saw that it is possible that in the future the production of cultivated meat may come to cause less harm to animals than even the production of plants (because of the deaths of animals in planting and harvesting procedures). Therefore, animal advocates should be in favor of cultivated meat.

Finally, the third debate listed some important points to take into account when assessing how much animal activists should focus on cultivated meat compared to focusing on other kinds of strategy. We saw that activism focused on technological change (as is the case with cultivated meat) does not replace antispeciesist educational activism, but that, if combined with it, it offers good opportunities for positive change and prevents setbacks for animals.

Finally, we also saw that, although at present the use of cultivated meat technology is focused on reducing animal exploitation, it has the potential in the future to be used also to reduce the harms animals endure as a result of natural processes, especially with regard to predation. Of course, there may be other, more efficient ways of reducing the suffering of wild animals, including suffering that results from predation, than investing in cultivated meat technology. One example is reducing primary productivity[132]. Regardless of this, however, cultivated meat proves to be a very promising technology in terms of reducing the suffering and deaths of animals, whether those exploited by humans or those outside human control.

## Volume IX: Ethics and the Future

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/

### Future Risks for Sentient Beings: An Introduction

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/01-future-risks-for-sentient-beings-an-introduction.html

#### 1.1 The past, the present, and the future

The emergence of factory farming in the 1930s and its subsequent large-scale application resulted in an enormous multiplication of two things: (1) the number of animals killed and subjected to living a life of suffering; (2) the levels of suffering for each animal. In short, factory farming multiplied the harms humans cause to other animals on a scale never seen before.

At the beginning of the twentieth century, animal advocates probably would not have imagined that factory farming would emerge just a few decades later. However, at that time there were already clues that the technology then emerging would result in factory farming.

Now consider two thought experiments[1].

*(1) You, going from the present to the past *

Imagine that you could go back in time and warn those people that something terrible was about to emerge. Perhaps there would be time to prevent factory farming from emerging (or at least to reduce its negative impact). Of course, it might be too late to try anything. But imagine that your time machine allowed you to go back to well before the beginning of the twentieth century. It seems that the earlier you managed to go back, the greater your chances of preventing the catastrophe (or at least of minimizing its negative impact), since the people you influenced would have more time to try.

*(2) You, coming from the future to the present *

Now imagine that you are once again a time traveler, but this time from the future. Imagine that you have come from the year 4025 to warn the people of the present that things are about to emerge

in the future so terrible that they would make even factory farming look like "a tiny grain of sand" by comparison. As in the previous example, there is a reason for you to come back to the present moment. At first you tried going back to times closer to 4025, but you saw that your efforts would be futile: it was necessary to go back to earlier times to allow enough time to prevent the catastrophes. For this reason, you ended up in the present time.

What these thought experiments aim to ask is: with regard to the bad things that could emerge for sentient beings[2] in the future, are we now perhaps in the same position that animal advocates were in before the emergence of factory farming? As we will see below, this is what the concept of *s-risks* is about: suffering on a gigantic scale that could arise in the future, and what to do to prevent it.

#### 1.2 What are s-risks?

At present, a very large number of nonhuman animals suffer intensely, and in many cases in ways that did not exist in the past. Likewise, in the future new ways of harming sentient beings on a massive scale may emerge, on a scale vastly greater than anything that has existed so far.

One concept used to address this problem is that of *risks of future suffering* (usually abbreviated as *s-risks*). This concept concerns the possibility that suffering will be massively increased in the future[3], and it can be defined as follows:

- *S-risks:* risks that events will occur in the future that result in suffering of gigantic magnitude[4], exceeding the suffering that has existed on Earth so far.
The concept of s-risks is centered on suffering, but there could be an analogous concept to address all the forms of harm that animals could endure, and not only suffering

(such as, for example, the harm of death). In that case, there could be a concept such as *h-risks* (risks of future harm). However, in this book we will speak of s-risks because that is the concept that has been widely used in the debate on these questions, even though, technically speaking, *h-risks* would be a more appropriate term, since it is more comprehensive.

#### 1.3 Differences between s-risks and x-risks

*S-risks* are a different concept from *x-risks* (*existential risks*). Both s-risks and x-risks are about the long term and astronomical impacts. But whereas x-risks are about risks of the annihilation of humanity (or at least of a drastic reduction in its potential), s-risks are about scenarios involving astronomical suffering (and it is therefore a concept that necessarily takes into account all sentient beings).

Certain s-risks may also be x-risks, but there are s-risks that are not x-risks. For example, there are forms of suffering inflicted on nonhuman sentient beings that do not harm humans, and that may even promote certain human interests (the consumption of animals is an example).

#### 1.4 Measuring the seriousness of an s-risk

Every s-risk concerns risks of suffering of astronomical magnitude, but each s-risk has a different degree of *seriousness*. This is because not only does the *severity* of each s-risk vary (for example, the number of victims who would potentially be affected and how much each one would suffer), but the *probability* of each s-risk materializing also varies.

Thus, one way to measure the *seriousness* of an s-risk is to multiply *how bad the outcome would be* by its *probability of occurring* (this would reveal its *expected disvalue*, or ED)[5].

This calculation reveals something important about s-risks. Since s-risks are, by definition, many orders of magnitude greater than current suffering (even compared with animal exploitation combined with the suffering of animals in the wild), the ED of each s-risk is enormous, even when the probability of its occurring is small.

#### 1.5 S-risks and new technologies

One factor that can give rise to s-risks is the emergence of new technologies. This risk is great especially if the technology would benefit those who hold it and they have no moral consideration for the beings negatively affected by it. If humanity has advanced technology but moral progress does not occur in parallel, there is a great risk that this will result in suffering of unprecedented magnitude.

As we have seen, one past example of how the emergence of a technology massively multiplied the suffering and deaths of sentient beings was the advent of factory farming (which, in turn, was a result of industrialization). Another example was the development of new weapons technologies.

If human extinction or a collapse of civilization does not occur, technology will probably continue to advance, perhaps making it possible to colonize planets and even billions of galaxies. Thus, technologies with a vastly greater impact may emerge in the future, which also increases the chances that their negative impact will be vastly greater.

For scenarios of astronomical suffering to occur, it is not necessary for the agents to intend to harm the victims: it is enough that they do not care (or care very little) about them, as happens with the act of consuming animal products, for example. New technologies, together with indifference, are already enough to considerably increase the probability that suffering of colossal size will be caused.

Moreover, it may also happen that the agents intend to use the technology to harm the victims. Or, again, suffering on a massive scale may arise accidentally. It is also possible that agents allow or promote the victims' suffering of natural harms when they could have prevented it. In short, there are many ways in which an s-risk could arise. We will see more about this below.

#### 1.6 Classification of s-risks according to how they arise

S-risks can be classified according to various parameters. In this section, we will see how they can be classified according to the way they arise, following the classification given by Baumann (2022, p.13-9). In the next section, we will look at other parameters.

#### 1.6.1 Incidental s-risks

These occur when ways of achieving a certain goal generate a great deal of suffering, but without the suffering being sought for its own sake. The agents may simply be indifferent, or may even prefer an alternative without suffering, but not be willing to pay the costs.

Some examples:

- *Suffering as an effect of high productivity*. A present-day example is factory farming. In the future, similar scenarios may occur, but on a much larger scale.
- * Suffering for the sake of gaining information*. A present-day example is animal experimentation. An example in the future would be the creation of virtual simulations with digital sentient beings to gain knowledge about how sentient beings behave.
- *Suffering for entertainment*. Just as there are bullfights today, new kinds of sentient beings may be created in the future for similar forms of entertainment.
#### 1.6.2 Agential s-risks

These occur when the agent aims to cause the harm. Let us look at some examples:

- *Sadists*. Future technologies may multiply their potential to cause harm.
- *Feelings of hatred*. A tribal "us vs. them" mentality can result in hatred against those who belong to a certain ethnicity, religion, political ideology, etc.
- *Extreme punishments*. Past examples are the forms of punishment that were applied precisely because they caused extreme suffering.
A key factor in the increase of agential s-risks is the presence of malevolent traits (*narcissism*, *psychopathy*, *Machiavellianism*, and *sadism*) in powerful individuals[6].

#### 1.6.3 Natural s-risks

These arise without the action of agents. For example, independently of human action, natural processes already harm animals to an extremely high degree, tending to maximize the number of sentient beings who are born to have lives full of suffering[7]. For every animal who manages to survive, literally thousands or even millions are born only to experience suffering and die prematurely. The norm in the wild is for them to be victims of malnutrition, hunger, and thirst, disease, physical injuries, psychological stress, hostile weather events, natural disasters, and interspecific, intraspecific, and sexual conflicts.

These animals are the vast majority of sentient beings on Earth. For example, if we compare the populations of animals exploited by humans and of animals in the wild and draw an analogy with the span of one year, the former would represent only 14 seconds of the year[8]. All the rest (364 days, 23 hours, 59 minutes, and 46 seconds) would be animals in the wild. *Natural s-risks* are the risks that suffering resulting from natural causes will expand on an astronomical scale.

This suffering is a result of the way natural selection works. For example, the trait of maximizing the number of offspring offers a great advantage in transmitting genetic information: with such gigantic broods (with thousands or even millions of offspring, depending on the species), it is highly likely that at least one or two will survive and reproduce, passing this trait on. However, in stable populations, on average only one offspring survives per adult[9] (that is, two per brood). All the rest are born almost solely to experience the suffering associated with death.

If this maximization of suffering is a result of natural selection, then, if there are other

planets where sentient life has developed, it is likely that this has also happened there and continues to happen.

There is also a risk that humans will in the future expand this suffering (for example, by spreading life beyond Earth). Although this would already be an incidental s-risk, it would also, indirectly, be a natural s-risk.

#### 1.7 Other classifications

S-risks can be classified according to various other parameters, and not only according to the way they arise. Below are some other possible classifications[10]:

- *Known and unknown s-risks*. These depend on whether or not we are currently able to imagine them (for example, in the Middle Ages no one imagined that the atomic bomb would come about).
Unknown s-risks can also be subclassified according to the way they arise:

- *Incidental: *when unknown mechanisms will lead to incidental s-risks.
- *Agential: *agents may come to have reasons in the future to cause harm that we do not yet know about.
- *Natural: *the universe may already contain much more suffering than we think.
Other parameters according to which s-risks can be classified are:

- *According to the type of sentient being affected*. For example, whether or not it is human, whether or not it is organic, etc.
- *Whether or not they can be influenced*. That is, whether or not it is possible to do something to prevent or minimize them. Here, however, it is important to distinguish between: (1) scenarios that, given the laws of physics, it is impossible to influence and (2) scenarios that cannot currently be influenced but may become open to influence in the future.
There may be many other parameters according to which s-risks can be classified. The list above should not be seen as complete.

Below we will look at some concrete examples of s-risks.

#### 1.8 Some examples of s-risks

In the debate about the future, there is a concern with trying to estimate what the main s-risks are and how to prevent them (or at least how to make them occur to a lesser extent). Let us look below at three possible scenarios of massive suffering in the future and the risk factors that could give rise to them. The risk factors will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 8. In Chapter 9 we will look at some strategies for preventing them.

Important: since it is difficult to estimate the probability of the future turning out one way or another, the following examples are well-informed guesses, but they are not necessarily the s-risks most likely to occur. Moreover, all of these examples may still be a small fraction of s-risks, compared with the s-risks still unknown.

S-risks can arise from a wide range of scenarios. Therefore, we must be careful with the availability heuristic, which is the bias that leads us to think that the cases we remember most easily are necessarily the most representative. This bias can lead us to think, mistakenly, that the s-risks we remember most easily will necessarily be the most likely.

With this in mind, here are some examples.

#### 1.8.1 An increase in animal exploitation

There are at least three ways in which the suffering caused by animal exploitation could come to be massively increased:

- Expanding it in scale (that is, affecting a greater number of sentient beings).
- Making it qualitatively worse (that is, increasing the harms suffered by each animal).
- Creating new ways in which it can happen.
One example of an s-risk of this kind that has materialized is the use of insects for consumption, which emerged at the end of the twentieth century and has been expanding in several countries[11]. Since these animals are very small, producing an equivalent amount of meat requires a vastly greater number of individuals to suffer and die[12]. Moreover, invertebrates are typically disregarded even more than other nonhuman animals. This degree of disregard magnifies the negative effect on each invertebrate. For example, the space allotted to insects on farms is extremely small, even smaller, in proportion to their size, than that given to other animals[13].

#### 1.8.2 The expansion of wild animal suffering

An increase in the suffering of wild animals may occur owing to an increase in the number of animals on Earth (as with *rewilding*[14] practices, which aim to return ecosystems to their state prior to human presence) or owing to the intentional or accidental spread of life beyond it (as in panspermia[15] and terraforming[16]).

These practices may be good from an environmentalist point of view or an anthropocentric one, but they are very negative for the animals affected. As we have seen, natural processes tend to maximize the number of animals who live lives full of suffering and die prematurely. This happens on a gigantic scale, much larger even than that of animal exploitation[17], and it happens to a greater extent the greater the amount of plant biomass available, since this implies an increase in the number of reproductions, which, in turn, is directly linked to the maximization of suffering[18]. Given the prevalence of the environmentalist view and the disregard for the good of animals, the expansion of natural territory and of life are usually seen as entirely positive. For the animals affected by such practices, however, their effects are predominantly negative[19].

#### 1.8.3 The creation of new forms of sentience

The creation of new forms of sentience may also give rise to vast amounts of suffering, especially if there is a high probability that these beings will not receive moral consideration. Examples of risks of this kind are the creation of genetically modified animals and, especially, the creation of nonbiological forms of sentience[20].

The possibility of nonbiological sentience exists because perhaps sentience appears whenever any physical structure is organized in such a way as to provide the conditions for it to appear, regardless of whether or not the structure is organic. One way to understand this possibility is through the following thought experiment.

Let us imagine that our neurons were gradually replaced by nonorganic neurons. If our sentience did not fade as the neurons were replaced, and if we remained sentient after all the neurons had been replaced, this would suggest that it is possible for nonorganic beings to be sentient in the future, should they come to have a structure organized so as to perform the same functions as a brain.

This possibility is an s-risk because, if these beings come to exist, there is a high probability that they will not receive moral consideration because they are not organic, and will then be harmed in all sorts of ways, just as nonhuman animals are today. The very mistaken idea held by many animal activists, that animals should be respected because they are animals or because they are living beings (and not because they are sentient), is a factor that has the potential to result in disregard for nonorganic sentient beings.

In the future, nonorganic sentience could arise not only through digital modifications of biological bodies, but also, for example, in sentient simulations within a computer program. Such beings, although sentient, might have no faces and might neither move nor scream. So it might be hard to feel empathy for them[21]. If such beings come to exist, humans will probably not care about them, just as happens with animals (or perhaps it will be even worse, since animals are already very similar to humans and yet,

even so, most humans do not care much about them). It may also happen that a digital entity is already sentient at a certain point without our noticing (and that we then cause it suffering without realizing it).

If nonorganic sentience is possible, enormous numbers of digital sentient beings may come to exist in the future, since creating them may involve far lower costs than creating biological sentient beings. Just as anyone can copy computer programs at will today, it is possible that in the future anyone will be able to create digital sentient beings.

Thus, the potential for vast numbers of digital sentient beings, together with a lack of consideration, poses a serious s-risk (exactly as happens in animal agriculture, all the more so since both are combined with economic incentives).

For this reason, it is important to combat not only speciesism, but also *substratism*. Just as *speciesism* is discrimination based on the species to which someone belongs, *substratism* is discrimination based on the type of substrate that makes up a being's body (for example, whether it is organic or nonorganic). Just as *anthropocentrism* is a form of *speciesism* (which discriminates against those who do not belong to the human species), *carbonism* is a form of *substratism* (which discriminates against those who are not organic).

Substratism, just like speciesism, can produce suffering in astronomical amounts in the future. That is why it is important to emphasize that animals should be considered because they are sentient (and not because they are animals or because they are living beings), and that this implies considering nonorganic sentient beings, should they come to exist.

#### 1.9 Conclusion

The risks that the scenarios mentioned above will materialize are not trivial. In fact, they are very great, since it is easy to ignore such problems and, moreover, they are not being discussed. For this reason, it is extremely necessary to begin a broad debate on s-risks.

### Temporal Impartiality: What It Is and Why It Matters

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/02-temporal-impartiality-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters.html

#### 2.1 Introduction

The way our decisions may affect the sentient beings who will live in the distant future is still a greatly neglected question, though it has begun to receive attention[22].

Below, we will look at one of the central reasons this question has been neglected (the presence of *temporal bias*) and at the reasons for adopting an approach centered on *temporal impartiality*[23]. We will also see that, even if someone rejects temporal impartiality, this is not enough to justify dismissing a strong concern with how our decisions will affect future sentient beings.

#### 2.2 Temporal bias

Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of flawed reasoning, or mental shortcuts that cloud our judgment. One of the factors that leads people to neglect the impact of their decisions on future beings is *temporal bias*, which consists in the tendency to give less importance to an event depending on how far from the present it lies.

To understand why this tendency is a bias, we need only remember that the moment that is now the present was once the future, and that the coming future moments will also come to pass, just as this moment did. An example of temporal bias would be to think that, 10 years ago, we should not have cared about ensuring that the moment we are living now would not be bad for us, merely because at that time it was far off in time.

How hard we should strive to bring about or avoid a certain event ought to depend on how good or bad it is, not on how near to or far from the present it is. Thus, rejecting temporal bias means accepting that no moment in time, in itself, has a higher or lower status (what matters is how good or bad the event would be). This can be better understood through the idea of *temporal impartiality*, which is an implication

of the more general idea of impartiality. We will look at these concepts below.

#### 2.3 Impartiality

- *Impartiality:* the unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions.
Impartiality[24] implies that harms and benefits of equal magnitude must be given the same weight, regardless of arbitrary factors such as the race, gender, or species of those affected by the decision, or any other factor that is the result of the natural lottery.

It also implies that someone is unfairly disfavored not only when they are disregarded entirely, but also when, on the basis of arbitrary factors, their good is given less weight.

As we will see below, temporal impartiality is one specific application of this general idea of impartiality.

#### 2.4 Temporal impartiality

To understand the idea of *temporal*[25] impartiality, it helps to compare it with the idea of *spatial* impartiality.

We saw above that impartiality implies rejecting arbitrary distinctions, such as giving different degrees of moral consideration on the basis of the species, race, or gender of those affected by the decision. Another example of an arbitrary distinction would be to give different degrees of moral consideration depending on where someone happens to be. Thus, impartiality implies spatial impartiality:

- *Spatial impartiality:* the unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions, regardless of where they are located.
One implication of spatial impartiality is that there is no justification for giving less weight to the good of a sentient being just because that being is far away from us.

Note that spatial impartiality is not an idea distinct from impartiality in general: it is merely an *implication* of it. However, impartiality also implies the same with respect to time:

- *Temporal impartiality*: the unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions, regardless of the time in which they exist.
Thus, one implication of temporal impartiality is that there is no justification for giving less weight to the good of a sentient being just because that being will exist in the future (whether near or distant). The important practical conclusion is this: according to temporal impartiality, the fact that a harm will occur in the distant future does not weaken the reasons for preventing it.

Most people who aim to reduce suffering in the world think of the individuals alive today (one of the reasons for this, besides temporal bias, is that it is hard to empathize with individuals who will exist in the distant future). However, if what we have seen makes sense, giving someone less consideration depending on the time in which they will exist is analogous to discriminating against them on the basis of where they live, their species, skin color, gender, and so on.

This, in short, is the central idea of temporal impartiality.

#### 2.5 The objection that future beings are merely potential beings

One objection to temporal impartiality holds that future individuals are, for now, mere possibilities that may never come to exist, unlike individuals who already exist. According to this objection, for this reason future individuals should either not count morally or be given less weight.

One response to this objection is to point out that our decisions can cause such possibilities to become real individuals in the future, and can also make their lives more positive or more negative. For example, even those who hold that there is no duty to bring new sentient beings into existence to have positive lives can recognize that there is a duty not to bring new sentient beings into existence to have negative lives. They can also recognize that, if a being will necessarily exist in the future regardless of what we decide, we should decide now in a way that avoids harming it and seeks to benefit it. These points will be discussed in more detail in the next chapter.

Thus, there are at least two ways in which our decisions can affect future beings:

- Our decision may determine whether or not a future sentient being comes to exist, and whether it is born into a context in which it will probably have a predominantly negative or positive life.
- Our decision may not determine whether or not a future sentient being comes to exist, but may determine the number of negative or positive events it will have in its life.
A good part of animal advocacy is already about future beings. For example, veganism is mostly about trying to prevent more animals from being born to lead lives full of suffering, not about animals who already exist. This is also the goal of sterilization programs, whether for wild or domesticated animals. Regulations that try to make exploited animals suffer less, in turn, are about ensuring that beings who will necessarily come to exist suffer less during their lives. Finally, spreading a view that gives consideration to all sentient beings aims mainly at increasing, from then on, the likelihood that future sentient beings will have lives with more positive events and fewer negative ones. Of course, part of animal advocacy is about helping animals who already exist. Examples include programs for vaccinating animals and treating diseases, helping animals in fires and other natural disasters, caring for orphaned animals, rescuing trapped animals, and programs for meeting animals' basic needs. However, as we have seen, a good part of animal advocacy already stems from recognizing that future beings deserve consideration.

One way to see that it is arbitrary to give less weight to someone's good depending on how far into the future they will exist is to imagine what we would think if generations before ours had believed there was nothing wrong with actions that would harm us enormously, simply because at the time we did not yet exist.

The veil of ignorance thought experiment can also help ground the idea of temporal impartiality[26]. Imagine that we had to decide which principles of justice people should follow, but without knowing in which era we would be born (knowing only that we would have to be born in some era). Under such conditions, it seems we would argue for giving equal consideration to all individuals who might be affected by agents' decisions, no matter in which era they would exist.

#### 2.6 Does rejecting temporal impartiality justify disregarding future beings?

What we have seen above suggests that there are strong reasons to accept temporal impartiality and to give equal consideration to the beings who will exist in the future.

However, let us imagine that there were a justification for giving greater weight to the good of the sentient beings who exist now. Well, this would not show that there is a justification for disregarding future beings: there would only be a justification for giving them less weight.

And even if that were the case, we should still give enormous importance to the long-term future, to the point of prioritizing it over the present and the short-term future. This may sound strange at first. Below is an explanation of why this implication follows.

The future may last for many eons, and therefore the number of sentient beings who may exist over the course of the future would also be immense. The point is this: that number would be so immense that, even if we gave less and less weight to each sentient being depending on how far into the future it will exist, we would still have to conclude in favor of prioritizing concern for the long-term future, given the total number of individuals affected. This is one of the central arguments for a focus on the long term, which we will examine in Chapter 4.

#### 2.7 Conclusion

If what we have seen above makes sense, then we must draw two important conclusions, if our goal is to make the world contain less suffering:

(1) We need to consider all sentient beings (including those of the distant future). (2) We need to give great weight to the long-term future.

Two factors have contributed greatly to the neglect of this important question. One of them, as we have seen, is temporal bias. The other is speciesism. The combination of these two factors contributes to the following result, which is a double neglect:

(1) Because of speciesism, when concern for the long-term future does appear, usually only future humans are taken into account.

(2) Because of temporal bias, those who already accept considering all sentient beings (for example, animal advocates) have usually disregarded future sentient beings.

If our goal is for there to be less suffering in the world, we need to reject this double neglect. Concern for the long term needs to reject speciesism and consider all sentient beings, and concern for sentient beings needs to reject temporal bias and take the long-term future into account[27].

**Notes**
