[23] For a detailed discussion of these topics, see Parfit (1984, p. 351-443);
[24] For an introduction to the implications of impartiality for decisions that affect nonhuman sentient beings, see Animal Ethics (2015, 2016). For a more detailed analysis, see Rowlands (2009 [1998], p. 118-175).
[25] Temporal impartiality is defended in Cowen; Parfit (1992). Its implications regarding s-risks are addressed in Baumann (2022, p. 22-3).
[26] On the veil of ignorance, see chapter 10 of Volume II of this collection. See also Animal Ethics (2016).
[27] For an argument defending these two theses in detail, see O'brien (2023).

### The Objection That Future Beings Are Merely Potential Beings

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/03-the-objection-that-future-beings-are-merely-potential.html

#### 3.1 The objection that we should care only about beings who already exist

We saw in the previous chapter that one of the most common objections to concern for the long-term future is based on the idea that future sentient beings are merely *potential beings*, that is, beings who do not yet exist and who may perhaps never come to exist. According to this objection, for this reason we should care only about beings who already exist.

Now consider the following causes:

- Spreading veganism.
- Pursuing regulations to make exploited animals suffer less.
- Protecting abandoned animals.
- Working to reduce the suffering of wild animals.
According to the objection, fighting for these causes makes sense because "they are about helping those who already exist." By contrast, the objection maintains, concern for the long-term future makes no sense, because it concerns beings who may never even come to exist.

This objection is sometimes raised especially in connection with concern about the possibility that nonorganic sentient beings may emerge in the future. According to the objection, we should not worry about this because it is something that may never even happen. Organic sentient beings, on the other hand, the objection concludes, already exist, and so we should care about them.

Is this a plausible objection? That is what we will discuss in this chapter.

#### 3.2 Should we care only about sentient beings who already exist?

A first way to challenge this objection is to question the assumption that we should care only about the sentient beings who have existed up to now. For example, it could be pointed out that, if the reason for caring about already existing sentient beings is the possibility that our decisions may affect them positively or negatively, then we have the same reason to care about sentient beings who do not yet exist but who may come to exist (since our decisions can also affect them positively or negatively).

It could be objected that, if no one has a duty to bring new sentient beings into existence, but we do have a duty not to kill those who already exist, this is because we have duties only toward individuals (and not toward future *possibilities* of individuals). Thus, the objection concludes, we have no obligations regarding how our decisions affect future beings.

However, someone could agree that we have no obligations toward future possibilities of individuals and still disagree that we have no obligations regarding how our decisions affect future beings.

First, someone could hold that we have a duty to make the history of the world from now on contain as many sentient beings with positive lives as possible. This duty would not be a duty toward this or that future possibility of a sentient being, but rather an *impersonal *duty to bring about the best consequences[28].

Second, and more importantly, even if someone denies the duty to bring new sentient beings into existence, we could still have at least two kinds of duties toward future beings:

- Not to bring new sentient beings into existence to live lives full of suffering.
- If a future sentient being will necessarily exist, to try to make its life contain less suffering than it otherwise would.
Both duties could be recognized even by those who reject a duty to make future possibilities of sentient beings come to be realized[29]. And, contrary to what might seem at first, as will be explained in the next section, these two duties are

the central focus of veganism, of attempts to make exploited animals suffer less, of the protection of abandoned animals, and also of the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals.

#### 3.3 The struggle for animals is usually already a struggle for possible future beings

We saw that the objection under discussion assumes that causes such as veganism, attempts to make exploited animals suffer less, the protection of abandoned animals, and the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals make sense because "they are about sentient beings who already exist." Meanwhile, the objection maintains, concern for the long-term future makes no sense because "it is about beings who do not yet exist (and who may never come to exist)."

However, this is mistaken. Each of those causes is also mostly about consideration for future beings. We will look at this point for each of them below:

The central goal of veganism is not to help animals who already exist, but rather to reduce the number of animals who would be born to lead lives full of suffering and to be killed. Veganism is therefore a recognition of the duty not to bring new sentient beings into existence to live lives full of suffering.

Now consider attempts to regulate animal exploitation so that animals suffer less. For the sake of argument, let us set aside the discussion of whether these regulations really reduce the suffering of such animals. Suppose they do. Even if that is the case, by the time a regulation comes into force, the animals who will benefit from it are generally not those who had already been born when the regulation was proposed. Of course, there may be some exceptions, as in the case of cows and sows who are exploited for several years. However, the vast majority of animals are killed within days or, at most, months. Thus, activists who pursue such regulations are recognizing a duty, if a sentient being will exist in the future, to try to make its life contain less suffering than it otherwise would.

Let us now consider the case of protecting abandoned animals, such as dogs and cats. Again, some actions may be aimed at benefiting animals who already exist, as in the case of providing food, shelter, medical treatment, vaccination, or responsible adoption. However, one of the main focuses of advocacy in this area is precisely sterilization, aimed at preventing more animals from being born into such situations. This focus is, again, a recognition of the duty to prevent the birth of new sentient beings who would have lives full of suffering.

The same holds for the cause that aims to reduce the suffering of wild animals[30]. Again, in this case too, various actions aim to help animals who already exist, such as vaccinating animals and treating diseases, helping animals in fires and other natural disasters, caring for orphaned animals, rescuing trapped animals, and programs for meeting animals' basic needs. However, the vast majority of wild animals' suffering and premature deaths results from their enormous reproductive rates[31]. Most species of animals in the wild reproduce in broods containing anywhere from thousands to many millions of offspring. For example, a single clutch of a common frog contains around 25,000 offspring[32]; that of octopuses, hundreds of thousands[33]; those of salmon, cod, and tuna, millions[34]; and that of the ocean sunfish reaches 300 million[35]. Terrestrial invertebrates can also lay hundreds, thousands, or even millions of eggs at a time[36]. In periods of roughly stable population, the average number of survivors from each brood is only two offspring (that is, one descendant per parent). All the rest are usually born only to experience the suffering of dying, without any positive experience. For this reason, the main focus of the proposal to reduce the suffering and premature deaths of wild animals is also to make fewer individuals be born into such conditions. It is, therefore, also a recognition of the duty to prevent new sentient beings from coming into existence to have lives full of suffering.

Thus, in all these struggles, the main focus is either to try to make beings who will exist in the future suffer less, or to try to prevent new sentient beings from coming to

exist to have lives full of suffering. In short, the animal cause is usually already about future beings. If so, then it makes no sense to claim that we should not care about the long-term future just because such concern would be about beings who do not yet exist and who may never come to exist. In concern for the long-term future, the goal is likewise to try to make beings who will exist in the future suffer less and to try to prevent new beings from coming to exist to have lives full of suffering (and, additionally, depending on the strand, to bring new beings into existence to have positive lives). This holds whether we are talking about possible future organic or nonorganic sentient beings.

**Notes**

[28] This position is known as the *total view*. On this, see Singer (2002[1993], p. 111-115) and Višak (2013, p. 71-8).
[29] This position is known as the *prior existence view*. On this, see Singer (2002[1993], p. 111-115) and Višak (2013, p. 71-8).
[30] For the philosophical foundations of this cause, see Cunha (2022).
[31] For a detailed explanation of this, see Horta (2010).
[32] Rastogi *et al.* (1983).
[33] Boyle and Rodhouse (2005).
[34] Baum and Meister (1971); Hinckley (1987).
[35] Froese; Luna (2004).
[36] Brueland (1995).

### What Reasons Are There to Focus on the Long Term?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/04-what-reasons-are-there-to-focus-on-the-long-term.html

#### 4.1 What is longtermism?

The word *longtermism*[37] is used to express different ideas, depending on the author. Sometimes it is used to refer to a *goal*. At other times, it is used to refer to a *practical focus* for trying to achieve that goal[38]. Below, two kinds of goals (one longtermist and one short-termist) and two practical focuses (one longtermist and one short-termist) are compared.

- *Longtermist goal:* aims to have the best possible impact on history from now until the end of time. This goal necessarily implies giving equal weight to every moment in time (that is, it implies temporal impartiality).
However, two people who agree on the longtermist goal may disagree about what we should focus on in practice to best achieve it. Thus, there are at least two kinds of practical focus for achieving the longtermist goal:

- *Longtermist practical focus:* to have the best possible impact on history from now until the end of time, we should focus on the impact our decisions will have on the long-term future.
- *Short-termist practical focus:* to have the best possible impact on history from now until the end of time, we should focus on the impact our decisions will have at the present moment or in the near future.
Now consider the short-termist goal:

- *Short-termist goal:* aims to have the best possible impact on the present or the near future. This goal will give less weight to (or even entirely neglect) the distant future (that is, it rejects temporal impartiality).
Since the short-termist goal does not seek to have an impact on the long-term future, there is only one kind of practical focus for achieving it:

- *Short-termist practical focus:* to have the best possible impact on the present or the near future, we should focus on the impact our decisions will have at the present moment or in the near future.
We thus have the following possibilities:

- Longtermist goal with a longtermist practical focus
- Longtermist goal with a short-termist practical focus
- Short-termist goal with a short-termist practical focus
#### 4.2 What will we see in this chapter?

In section 4.3 we will look at the central reason for adopting a longtermist goal. In section 4.4 we will look at arguments for adopting a longtermist practical focus. In section 4.5 we will look at the main objections to the longtermist practical focus and how these objections can be answered.

#### 4.3 Why adopt a longtermist goal?

The central reason for adopting a longtermist goal is this: if what matters to us is the good of all the beings we may affect, the question we ask will not be "how can we have the best impact on the present world or the near future?" but rather "how can we have the best impact on history from now on?". A more detailed defense of this idea can be found in Chapter 2.

#### 4.4 Reasons for a longtermist practical focus

As we have seen, the practical focus on the long term holds that, to have the best impact on history from now on, we should focus on the long-term consequences of our decisions.

The main reason for the practical focus on the long term is that, unless there is a mass extinction of sentient life, it is very likely that there will be far more sentient beings in the distant future than in the present or the near future, both *diachronically* and *synchronically*:

- *Diachronically* because the future may be immensely long. The individuals alive now or in the near future are very few compared with those who will live in the coming centuries, millennia, eons, and so on.
- *Synchronically* because the population of sentient beings at each moment may increase. For example, space colonization could multiply them by many orders of magnitude[39].
In short, depending on how we decide now, we will positively or negatively affect a gigantic number of beings who will exist over the course of the future.

Let us consider an analogy to better understand the practical focus on the long term. Imagine that someone has to choose between avoiding a certain suffering now or avoiding a certain suffering twenty years from now. Imagine, however, that the suffering that would occur twenty years from now would be much more intense and prolonged. If the person chooses to avoid the suffering of the present moment, they will make their life contain more suffering than if they had chosen the other option.

Analogously, if what we aim for is the best history of the world from now on for all sentient beings, we need to give equal weight to every moment. However, since the long-term future will contain far more sentient beings than the present moment or the short-term future, we have strong reasons to prioritize how our decisions affect the long-term future — this is the basic idea of the practical focus on the long term.

Interestingly, even if less and less weight were given to the good of each sentient being depending on how far into the future it will live, the number of sentient beings who may exist in the long-term future is so vast that we would still have to conclude in favor of prioritizing them, if our goal is the best complete history of the world. Thus, even those who reject temporal impartiality but still give some consideration to future beings would have to prioritize them.

Of course, how long the future will contain sentient beings and what the population of sentient beings will be at each moment is highly uncertain. But future beings vastly outnumber present ones *in expectation* (that is, multiplying their number by their probability of coming to exist), and this is enough for us to have strong reasons to care about them. This problem of uncertainty will be discussed below in section 4.5.3.

#### 4.5 The debate over the focus on the long term

Below, some of the most common objections to the practical focus on the long term will be discussed[40]:

#### 4.5.1 Is it better to leave future problems to future generations?

One objection to the practical focus on the long term holds that future generations will be better placed to solve future problems: they will know which s-risks[41] (that is, risks of suffering on a gigantic scale) are most serious and which strategies are best for preventing them. For the same reason, the objection concludes, we have an advantage in terms of knowledge if we focus on the present.

One possible response to this objection is to note that it is not guaranteed that future generations will know how to solve such problems. For example, if we leave it to future generations to investigate these problems, it may be too late to prevent the worst scenarios[42]. In

short, this response holds that the sooner we begin working on these problems, the sooner solutions to them will emerge, and that this will make history better from then on.

Moreover, even if future generations are better placed to solve such problems, this does not mean they will want to do so (since this will depend on how much consideration they give to sentient beings). So we should try to bring about both the *capacity *and the *will* to prevent suffering in the future.

It is sometimes claimed that the future will be better anyway thanks to moral progress and that, therefore, we need not worry. However, this is not guaranteed, since it depends crucially on what we do now to spread consideration for all sentient beings and on what continues to be done over time.

#### 4.5.2 Does focusing on the present have more influence?

Someone could accept that the good of future sentient beings counts equally but reject the practical focus on the long term because they believe we live in a crucial era for determining everything that will happen from now on. For example, certain events that will probably occur in the twenty-first century (such as the emergence of superintelligent, autonomous artificial intelligences) could have a disproportionate influence from then on. On this basis, it could be argued that, to have the best impact on the history of the world from now on, we should focus on the present (or, at least, on the near future).

One possible response here is to point out that we do not know how much influence each of these possible events will have on history from then on. For example, we do not know whether these will be the crucial events, whether others still unknown will be, or whether change will be gradual, with no crucial events. If we focus on particular events and they turn out not to have much influence on the future, we will have wasted our efforts[43]. Thus, it seems better to focus on investigating how our decisions can influence the future positively regardless of what happens. This can be done, for example, by investigating risk factors for s-risks and by planning broad strategies for preventing them.

#### 4.5.3 The objection that our degree of certainty about the present is greater

Another objection to the practical focus on the long term points out that the longer the time frame, the harder it is to predict the probability that an event will occur. For this reason, the objection holds, we should focus on the short term, since in that case our degree of certainty is greater.

However, the *degree of certainty* should not by itself determine how much we ought to focus on a scenario**. **Another crucial factor is the *magnitude of the scenario* (that is, how good or bad it is). Depending on how bad a scenario is, it may still be worth prioritizing its prevention, even if we are more uncertain about whether or not it will occur. One way of taking both *magnitude* and *degree of uncertainty* into account is to multiply one factor by the other, and the result is called *expected value* (or *expected disvalue*, if the result is negative[44]).

Let us look at an example. Imagine that we have to choose between preventing a negative event that could occur in the near future and preventing a negative event that could occur in the distant future. Imagine that we are able to estimate how negative each event would probably be, and that the near-future event would be -100 and the distant-future event would be -1000. However, imagine that the probability of the near-future event occurring is 80% and that, owing to uncertainty about the future, the probability of the distant-future event occurring is only 10%.

The expected disvalue of the near-future event would be -100 x 0.8 = -80. The expected disvalue of the distant-future event, on the other hand, would be -1000 x 0.1 = -100. Thus, according to the expected disvalue calculation, we would still have reason to prioritize preventing the distant-future event, even though the probability of its occurring is lower.

In short, what this response points out is that the magnitude of the long-term future is so vast that, even if there is great uncertainty about the future, it would still be worth prioritizing trying to influence it.

At this point it could be objected that the expected disvalue calculation could lead us to prioritize preventing scenarios that would be disastrous if they occurred, but whose probability of occurring is extremely remote.

There are at least two possible responses to this objection. The first is to acknowledge that it points to a problem with the formula for calculating expected disvalue, but to argue that the formula can be adapted to correct this problem. For example, instead of the factors *magnitude *of the harm and *probability* of occurrence having the same weight in the multiplication, the probability factor could be given greater weight.

The second response points out that there are strategies that tend to influence the future positively without requiring us to estimate the probability of the future turning out this way or that. Longtermist strategies fall into two broad groups: targeted and broad. Targeted strategies focus on preventing specific catastrophic scenarios. Broad strategies, by contrast, are designed to influence the future positively regardless of which scenarios occur. Thus, the objection in question could make sense only with respect to targeted strategies, but would not affect broad strategies.

One example of a broad strategy is to identify risk factors for s-risks and try to prevent them. We will see more about this below.

#### 4.5.4 The objection that the future is so uncertain that we have no way of deciding

A similar objection holds that the long-term future is so uncertain that we have not the slightest idea how our present decisions will affect it. For example, our influence will be diluted by the decisions of the many future agents[45]. The longer the future, the more is at stake, but also the smaller our influence. Thus, the objection concludes, the fact that the future is long is not enough to support the conclusion that we should focus on the long term.

However, there are things we can do now that tend to influence the long-term future positively even if we are highly uncertain about the future. For example, we can identify *risk factors*[46] for s-risks and try to

do things that reduce these risk factors. Risk factors are not themselves s-risks, but they greatly increase the probability that s-risks will come about.

The concept of risk factors is already widely used in medicine. For example, smoking, eating poorly, and not exercising are not, in themselves, diseases, but they greatly increase the probability of various diseases, even though they do not necessarily entail them. To know that it is good to avoid these risk factors, we do not need to know what each individual's health trajectory will be. Similarly, we can try to identify risk factors for s-risks and try to identify the actions that would help avoid them.

Some of the risk factors for s-risks are:

- Disregard for nonhuman sentient beings.
- Disregard for possible future nonbiological sentient beings[47].
- Demand for products and services whose production harms sentient beings.
- The prevalence of environmentalist values instead of concern for sentient beings.
- Human expansion and increasing technological power.
- Technological progress being much faster than moral progress[48].
Each of these risk factors will be addressed in more detail in Chapter 8.

#### 4.5.5 The objection that focusing on the long term would mean neglecting the present

Another common objection to the practical focus on the long term is to point out that it seems to imply neglecting present or near-future suffering, since this is vastly smaller in magnitude than possible long-term suffering.

One possible response here is to point out that, once again, there are actions we can take that tend to influence the whole of history from now on positively (for example, promoting the moral consideration of all sentient beings), and that, therefore, there is not necessarily a dilemma between addressing the long-term future and addressing the present.

At first glance, this may sound contradictory. Someone might ask, for example: "But aren't you defending the practical focus on the long term, then?". The answer is that some of the most promising strategies for the practical focus on the long term (such as advocating the moral consideration of all sentient beings) also help improve the short term.

#### 4.6 Conclusion

We have seen that the practical focus on the long term is one possible answer to the question "how can we have the best impact on the history of the world from now on?". We have also addressed some objections to this focus and the responses that have been given to them.

There seem to be good reasons in favor of the practical focus on the long term. However, another important conclusion here is that even those who reject this focus (and choose to give priority, for example, to the present or the near future) still have strong reasons to accept the longtermist *goal*, even if they do not accept the longtermist *practical focus*.

### Should We Focus on Preventing S-Risks or X-Risks?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/05-should-we-focus-on-preventing-s-risks-or-x-risks.html

#### 5.1 S-risks and x-risks

As we saw in Chapter 1, risks of future suffering, or *s-risks, *are the risks that events will occur in the future resulting in suffering on a gigantic scale, exceeding all the suffering that has existed on Earth so far[49]. Examples include the potential of future technology to vastly increase animal exploitation and the harms animals suffer as a result of natural processes[50], and to create new kinds of sentient beings, for example, in digital media[51].

Existential risks, in turn, also known as x-risks, are the risks of the annihilation of humanity (or, at least, of a collapse of civilization). Examples include global warming, nuclear weapons, pandemics, and so on.

To have the best impact on history from now on, should we focus on trying to prevent s-risks or x-risks? That is what we will discuss in this chapter.

#### 5.2 Discussing a speciesist attempt to defend the focus on x-risks

One way to defend the focus on x-risks is to argue that humans matter much more. However, there are two problems with this argument.

The first is that there seems to be no way to justify giving greater weight to humans. From an unbiased point of view, equal amounts of harm and benefit matter equally, regardless of factors that depend on luck, such as the species to which someone belongs.

The second problem is that, even if much less weight were given to

nonhuman sentient beings, the number of beings potentially affected by s-risks is so astronomically greater that we would still have to conclude in favor of investing more resources in preventing s-risks than x-risks.

#### 5.3 The claim that humanity is essential for preventing suffering

It is sometimes argued that we should prioritize preventing x-risks not because humans matter more, but because doing so would be necessary to prevent s-risks. In the absence of agents with technology at their disposal, there will be no one to reduce the suffering in the world. On this basis, it could be said that, as long as there are x-risks, we should not worry about s-risks. In short, what this argument holds is that the most important thing is to prevent s-risks, but that, to do so, we need to focus on preventing x-risks and forget about s-risks for the time being.

The strength of this argument depends on how positive or negative humanity's impact on history will be from now on. In the best scenario, humanity would continue to exist and try to prevent suffering. But another possibility is that it continues to exist and does not care about reducing the suffering that would already exist naturally or, worse still, produces much more suffering than would already exist naturally. Let us compare three possible scenarios:

(1) Humanity continues and there is less suffering than if it went extinct. (2) Humanity goes extinct. (3) Humanity continues and there is more suffering than if it went extinct.

It seems that 1 is the best of the three scenarios, and that 3 is worse than 2. The idea underlying the focus on preventing s-risks is that it is more important to avoid the worst scenario of all (in this case, scenario 3). Moreover, a strategy that is essential for avoiding the worst scenario (scenario 3) is also essential for trying to achieve the best scenario (scenario 1): spreading, as efficiently as possible, consideration for all sentient beings. This is crucial to ensure that, if humanity continues to exist, it will try to prevent suffering rather than increase it.

#### 5.4 The claim that we will obtain more resources if we prioritize humans

It is sometimes argued that, since people are speciesist, organizations whose goal is to benefit all sentient beings would gain more supporters and resources if they focused on human causes instead of on concern for all sentient beings. In short, what this argument means is that our goal should be to prevent harm to all sentient beings but that, curiously, the most efficient way to achieve this goal is to focus on humans.

A central problem with this argument is that it seems to overlook the fact that one of the main reasons why an astronomical amount of suffering is taking place, and why there is a great risk that it will be vastly multiplied in the future, is precisely the predominance of an anthropocentric view.

This is a very strong reason to prioritize advocating moral consideration for all sentient beings, and as soon as possible, since the non-acceptance of this idea is one of the main obstacles to the goal of preventing massive suffering in the world, both present and future suffering. For example, imagine that consideration for all sentient beings had begun to spread on a large scale two thousand years ago. There would probably be much less suffering than there is today.

If we advocate prioritizing humans, besides failing to spread consideration for all sentient beings, this will probably have the effect of reinforcing speciesism (or, at least, by not questioning it, of delaying changes in speciesist attitudes) and of being an obstacle to preventing the suffering that would occur from now on.

In short, it seems that the sooner (and the more widely) consideration for sentient beings is spread, the better the history of the world from now on is likely to be. One of the advantages of this strategy is that, if carried out carefully so as not to provoke rejection, it tends to influence the future positively, regardless of what might happen.

#### 5.5 Reasons to focus more on s-risks

Some reasons to focus more on preventing s-risks than x-risks are:

(1) Severity. Risks of future suffering have the potential to have an astronomically greater impact than existential risks, both in terms of *severity *(since they represent the possibility of extreme suffering throughout the entire lives of future sentient beings) and in terms of *scope *(since they would affect all sentient beings in the universe from now until the end of time).

(2) Expected impact. The probability of s-risks is not lower than that of x-risks.

(3) Tractability. There is also much that could be done to try to minimize s-risks.

(4) Degree of neglect: There are already many more people trying to prevent x-risks than s-risks.

Therefore, all the priority criteria point toward giving great importance to risks of future suffering.

However, it is also important to remember that the focus on s-risks or x-risks may be a matter of degree. That is, one goal does not necessarily exclude the other. Thus, believing that preventing x-risks is more important does not justify thinking that preventing s-risks is not very important. Likewise, if someone prioritizes s-risks, this does not mean they think preventing x-risks is not very important, and so on.

**Notes**

[50] On how animals are typically affected by natural processes and the ethical implications of this, see Cunha (2018, 2022) and Animal Ethics (2023 [2020]). On how this relates to s-risks, see Baumann (2022, p. 50-2, 56, 84 ) and Tomasik (2017, 2022).
[51] On this, see Tomasik (2015).

### Which Goals Should We Prioritize in the Long Term?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/06-which-goals-should-we-prioritize-in-the-long-term.html

#### 6.1 Different goals someone might want to achieve in the long term

Two people who agree that we should try to have the best impact on history from now on could disagree about what "having the best impact" means, depending on what they prioritize in terms of values.

For example, some people might have in mind preventing the extinction of the human species. Others, by contrast, might aim to prevent the future from containing astronomical amounts of suffering for sentient beings.

These are just two examples of goals someone might want to achieve in the long term. But there are many more possible goals. Here are some examples:

(1) Preventing suffering. (2) Preventing premature deaths. (3) Providing positive experiences to the beings who will exist. (4) Bringing about as many beings with positive lives as possible over time. (5) Preventing the extinction of humanity. (6) Maximizing human potential. (7) Preventing the extinction of sentient life.

Someone may consider that all of these goals should be pursued. However, it is also possible to think that only some of them should be pursued (or even only one of them).

Moreover, someone may believe that several of these goals (or even all of them) should be pursued, but with different degrees of importance. Below we will look at some arguments for prioritizing the first two (preventing suffering and preventing premature deaths). As should be clear, this does not necessarily mean discarding the other goals, since focusing on one goal rather than another may be a matter of *degree*.

What, then, does the choice to focus on this or that goal depend on? Below we will look at this discussion with respect to the focus on preventing suffering and, after that, we will discuss the focus on preventing premature deaths.

#### 6.2 What does the focus on preventing suffering depend on?

#### 6.2.1 Calculating how much to focus on preventing suffering

Consider the following questions:

(1) Should we place greater focus on preventing suffering? (2) If so, to what extent?

The answer to these questions depends on the answers we give to two other questions:

(1) *Weight*: what weight should we give to the goal of preventing suffering, compared with other goals? (2) *Expectation*: how optimistic or pessimistic should we be about the future?

The relationship between these two factors (*weight *and *expectation*) works as follows:

- The more optimistic someone is about the future, the more weight they have to give to the goal of reducing suffering in order to conclude that they should prioritize preventing suffering.
- Analogously, the more someone thinks the future has the potential to contain vast amounts of suffering, the less they need to have reducing suffering as their main goal in order to conclude that they should prioritize it.
One way to measure this is with the following formula[52]:

- *Degree of focus on suffering* (DFS): WS x ES.
- WS (*Weight of the goal of preventing suffering*): the more we value preventing suffering
relative to other goals, the higher the WS.

- ES (*Expectation of suffering*): the more we think the future may be full of suffering, the higher the ES.
The higher the DFS result, whether because we give greater weight to preventing suffering (high WS) and/or because we are pessimistic about the future (high ES), the more we will focus on preventing suffering.

#### 6.2.2 Applying the same reasoning to other goals

Although we have spoken above only of the focus on preventing suffering, the same reasoning applies to any other goal. It is always possible to multiply the weight we give to a goal by how much we expect that what it aims to prevent or achieve will occur.

For example, to know how much to focus on preventing premature deaths, we could multiply the weight we give to this goal compared with other goals by how many premature deaths we expect the future will probably contain.

Both examples above concerned focuses on preventing negative things (suffering and death). When the focus is on pursuing positive things (for example, providing positive experiences to sentient beings), although the weight axis remains the same (that is, the more weight we give to the goal of providing positive lives, the more we will focus on that goal), the expectation axis works the other way around (for example, the less we expect the future to contain positive experiences anyway, the more we will focus on that goal).

#### 6.3 Who could accept the focus on preventing suffering?

One might think that, to accept a focus on preventing suffering[53], one must have the prevention of suffering as one's only concern (or, at least, regard the prevention of suffering as a *trump* over any other goal). However, as is evident from the calculation above, this is not so. The focus on preventing suffering can be accepted by a much larger number of views. Listed below are the views that can accept this

focus.

(1) People whose *only goal* is to prevent suffering.

(2) People who also pursue other goals, but for whom preventing suffering is a *trump*. For these people, no matter how large the gain in other goals from the use of a certain resource, using it to prevent suffering would always take priority.

(3) People who also accept other goals, but for whom preventing suffering carries *greater weight* (even if it is not a trump). Unlike the people in item 2, for these people the balance may tip toward focusing on other goals if the gain in them from the use of a certain resource is large enough. However, in most situations these people would tend to focus on preventing suffering (especially if they are pessimistic about the future).

(4) People who give *equal weight* to other goals may prioritize preventing suffering if they are pessimistic about the future.

(5) People who give *greater weight to other goals* may still recognize that reducing suffering is an important goal (and may even prioritize it, depending on how pessimistic they are about the future).

#### 6.4 Some arguments for giving greater weight to the goal of preventing suffering

Below we will look at four arguments that have been offered for giving greater weight to the goal of preventing suffering compared with the goal of providing positive experiences[54]. It is important to note that these arguments do not compare the goal of preventing suffering with other goals that also concern preventing something negative (such as the goal of preventing premature death, which we will address in section 6.6). Here are the four arguments.

#### 6.4.1 The guarantee example (first version)

Imagine that we can guarantee one of these two things, but not both:

- If we are in extreme suffering, we will move to moderate suffering.
- If we are in moderate pleasure, we will move to extreme pleasure.
It seems more important to guarantee the first. This suggests that *reducing suffering* is more important than *increasing pleasure*.

#### 6.4.2 The guarantee example (second version)

Imagine that we can guarantee one of these two things, but not both:

- If we are in moderate suffering, we will not move to extreme suffering.
- If we are in extreme pleasure, we will not move to moderate pleasure.
Again, it seems more important to guarantee the first. This suggests that *preventing increases in suffering* is more important than *preventing decreases in pleasure*.

#### 6.4.3 The torture example

When someone is subjected to torture, they may end up turning against their loved ones or other innocents, betraying causes they believe in, or giving up their freedom or even their life. Yet many of these people would not do these same things in exchange for enormous pleasure. This suggests that suffering is far more unbearable than the lack of pleasure.

#### 6.4.4 The argument that preventing suffering better maximizes the positive balance

This last argument is not an argument for giving greater weight to preventing suffering, but it suggests that prioritizing the prevention of suffering is more efficient for achieving the goal of maximizing the total positive balance (that is, the total aggregate sum of pleasure minus suffering).

There are views according to which an additional unit of well-being has the same degree of importance, whether it is an increase in the well-being of someone who is suffering or of someone who is already well off[55]. According to these views, what we should do is try to maximize the total positive balance.

However, using a given amount of resources to improve the situation of those who are suffering is usually more efficient for maximizing the total positive balance[56]. For example, if someone has only five kilos of rice, giving them an additional kilo will make a more positive difference to their well-being than giving it to someone who already has, say, twenty kilos of rice.

Thus, the worse someone's situation, the more an additional unit of resources makes a positive difference to their well-being. Therefore, even someone who gives equal weight to producing what is positive (compared with preventing suffering) still has reasons to prioritize preventing suffering, since this would be more efficient for maximizing the total balance.

#### 6.5 How pessimistic about the future do we need to be in order to focus on suffering?

We will now discuss some arguments holding that we should be optimistic about the future[57]. We will also see that, in order to prioritize preventing suffering, we do not need to be highly pessimistic about the future (we need only recognize that the possibility of the future containing vast amounts of suffering is not negligible).

#### 6.5.1 The argument that technology will make causing suffering unnecessary

It is sometimes claimed that technology will make it easy to achieve what people want without needing to cause suffering. The idea is that, if people care at least a little about avoiding causing suffering, and the cost of avoiding it is low, they will avoid it. One example is the belief that cell-based meat will make animal exploitation obsolete, even if people do not care much about animals.

A first possible way to challenge this argument is to point out that perhaps the consideration most of these people give to animals is so low that they may not

be willing to pay the price of preventing animals' suffering, even if that price is minimal. For example, imagine that a point is reached at which cell-based meat is only slightly more expensive than conventional meat. Perhaps many people will not be willing to pay a few cents more for cultivated meat. And, even if cultivated meat becomes cheaper than conventional meat, perhaps many people will insist that they prefer the "original product." In short, the fact that someone does not aim at suffering for its own sake does not guarantee that they will try to prevent suffering, since the degree of moral consideration they give to those affected by their decisions may be very low, even if they do not aim at these victims' suffering.

Another way to respond to this argument is to point out that, even if it makes sense with respect to practices that produce suffering where the suffering is not aimed at for its own sake (such as the consumption of animals), technology can also increase the power of individuals whose goal is to cause suffering to others. Therefore, the possibility that technology may reduce the risks of unintended suffering is not enough for us to be optimistic about the future, especially since individuals with malevolent traits tend to seek and attain positions of power[58].

#### 6.5.2 The argument that things tend to get better

Another argument for optimism about the future is the claim that things have tended to get better over the last few centuries: a decline in violence, improvements in health such as cures for diseases, increased life expectancy, and so on.

However, this judgment only makes sense from an anthropocentric point of view. For example, there has been a gigantic increase in the number of exploited animals since the industrial revolution. This number continues to increase greatly, especially in the case of aquatic animals and invertebrates.

As for the suffering of wild animals, it is uncertain whether it has increased or decreased over time. For example, replacing green areas with urban development usually causes suffering and death to the animals who live there but, given the way natural processes typically affect animals[59], urbanization also prevents a gigantic

number of animals from being born only to suffer in such places[60].

The point is this: taking into account all the sentient beings affected, we do not know whether things are getting worse or better overall.

#### 6.5.3 The probability of s-risks is not negligible, and that is enough

To focus strongly on preventing suffering, we do not need a pessimistic view of the future. It is enough for us to believe that the probability of the future containing vast amounts of suffering is not negligible. This probability is far from negligible for three reasons[61]:

(1) Astronomical-scale suffering in the future could arise in many ways, and the future is very hard to predict. The probability that some of these ways will come about (including some we do not even envision today) is not negligible.

(2) Unless there is destabilization at a global level, technology is likely to keep developing. Those who hold power usually have insufficient (or even no) consideration for those affected by their decisions.

(3) So far, technologies have given us everything from cures for diseases to chemical weapons, nuclear bombs, and factory farming. So there is no guarantee that future developments will be used beneficially.

This has been a brief summary of the debate about focusing on the goal of preventing suffering. Next we will discuss the goal of preventing premature deaths.

#### 6.6 The goal of preventing premature deaths

The discussion of preventing harm to future sentient beings usually revolves around the goal of preventing suffering. This is because several of the leading authors on this question

are also proponents of ethical theories focused on preventing suffering[62]. However, another possible goal is preventing premature deaths. What reasons are there in favor of this goal? How should it be weighed against the goal of preventing suffering? This is what we will discuss below.

#### 6.6.1 How fortunate or unfortunate was someone in the life they had?

One of the reasons for thinking that preventing premature deaths is an important goal has to do with assessing how fortunate or unfortunate someone was in the life they had[63]. What factors should we base such an assessment on?

A first factor that immediately comes to mind is to examine how much suffering the life in question contained. This is certainly a relevant factor. However, the following example suggests that it is not the only relevant factor:

Suppose we could measure the amount of suffering someone had during their life. This would be obtained by adding up the moments of suffering and multiplying them by the intensity of the suffering at each moment (with "s" as the unit for measuring suffering). Imagine that we assessed the lives of Ana and Bia and obtained the following result:

- Ana had 200,000s
- Bia had 400,000s.
If we look only at suffering, we will say that Bia was more unfortunate in the life she had than Ana. However, imagine that Ana's suffering accounted for more than 95% of the experiences she had during her whole life, whereas Bia's life, despite containing twice as much suffering, had many more positive experiences, to the point that Bia's suffering did not even reach 50% of the total experiences she had during her life.

This example suggests that, in order to assess how fortunate or unfortunate someone was in the life they had, it is important to take into account not only the amount of suffering they experienced but also the amount of positive experiences. In other words, if the

aim is to assess *how good or bad* a life was for the one who lived it, one has to take into account both the negative and the positive events, not just the negative ones.

However, it can be misleading to rely on the *proportion* between these two factors. What matters is the *quantity* of these events (something that depends on *how long* someone lived). To make this point clearer, consider the following example.

Imagine that, when we assess the experiences Clara and Dora had during their lives, we find the following, in terms of proportion:

- Clara: 70% positive experiences and 30% negative experiences
- Dora: 60% positive experiences and 40% negative experiences
If we rely only on proportion, we will say that Clara was more fortunate in the life she had than Dora. However, imagine that Clara lived 20 years and Dora lived 80. Then Clara's 70% of positive experiences amounts to far fewer than Dora's 60% of positive experiences. This suggests that the *quantity* of positive and negative experiences (something that depends on *how much time* someone lived) is relevant, not only the proportion between positive and negative events.

We are now in a position to understand why premature deaths are events we have strong reasons to prevent: the more premature the death, the less opportunity there is for positive experiences to occur. Of course, it only makes sense to want someone to have more lifetime if there is a possibility that this life will be at least minimally meaningful. For this reason, the goal of preventing suffering is always an extremely important goal. However, it also makes sense to say that, if there is a possibility of a life being meaningful, premature death is a factor that contributes to someone being highly unfortunate in the life they had[64].

#### 6.6.2 Weighing the goal of preventing suffering against the goal of preventing death

We have seen that the goal of preventing deaths is directly related to the goal of providing

positive events. In section 6.4 we saw some examples suggesting that preventing suffering carries greater weight than obtaining positive experiences. However, it is important to note that those examples do not suggest that the goal of preventing suffering is a *trump*, since, depending on how much smaller the suffering is and how much greater the positive experience is, we might think it worth going through the suffering to attain the positive experience (learning to play a musical instrument is one example).

Moreover, the examples in section 6.4 weighed these two goals in situations that refer only to a given moment, asking us to imagine whether we would rather guarantee avoiding suffering or obtaining pleasure. Once we bring the time factor into the equation (which is directly related to preventing death), the weight of the goals of preventing suffering and obtaining positive experiences becomes more uncertain. Let us look at two examples of this.

- There are situations in which the suffering we would experience if we stayed alive is so great that we believe it is not worth continuing to live. This is the case, for example, of many terminally ill patients who ask to die in order to have their suffering relieved[65].
- On the other hand, there are situations in which we believe it is worth facing considerable (sometimes even very great) suffering if that is necessary to save our life (provided, of course, that there is a possibility of this life being at least minimally meaningful from then on).
These cases suggest that neither of these two goals (preventing suffering and preventing death) has priority over the other in all situations. They do suggest, however, that both goals are very important.

#### 6.7 Conclusion

There are several goals someone might want to achieve in terms of having the best long-term impact. If the arguments we have seen make sense, then even though there may be several goals worth pursuing, there are reasons to give extra weight to the goals of preventing suffering and preventing the premature deaths of sentient beings.

### What Does the Focus on S-Risks Consist Of?

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/07-what-does-the-focus-on-s-risks-consist-of.html

#### 7.1 Introduction

In this chapter we will address what Baumann (2022, p. 36-40) calls the *s-risk focus*. We will discuss how this focus relates to the way suffering may be distributed over the future, and what the difference is between an *s-risk focus* and a *narrow focus*.

As we have seen, *s-risks *are the risks that events will occur in the future resulting in suffering on a gigantic scale, exceeding all the suffering that has existed on Earth so far. It is sometimes argued that the most efficient way to prevent suffering in the history of the world from now on is to focus on preventing s-risks[66], since the magnitude of suffering in these cases may be so astronomical that it would make up most of future suffering. This is the so-called *s-risk focus*.

However, someone could have the goal of reducing future suffering as efficiently as possible but reject the s-risk focus because they believe that most future suffering will come from the sum of scenarios that are bad, but not bad enough to be s-risks. For this reason, we will now examine the probability of future suffering being distributed in one way or another.

#### 7.2 How will suffering probably be distributed over the future?

Baumann (2022, p. 37-8) observes that many phenomena have what is called a *heavy-tailed distribution *(in reference to the curve formed on the graph). For example, if we add up all the deaths from wars or earthquakes throughout history, most occurred in a small number of the worst cases. The same may hold for future suffering: a good percentage of it may be concentrated in the most extreme s-risks.

A distribution can be heavy-tailed to a greater or lesser degree. One reason for thinking that future suffering will be heavy-tailed to a high degree is that the scale of future suffering may vary by many orders of magnitude (for example, owing to the potential for

space colonization[67] or digital sentience[68]). So it could have extremely sharp peaks.

#### 7.3 The s-risk focus does not imply a narrow focus

Focusing on the worst cases does not mean focusing on just a few s-risks that someone considers the worst of all. This is so for the following reasons:

- Even if future suffering has a heavy-tailed distribution, this does not mean that most of the expected future suffering arises from a few specific cases of s-risks. It may arise from the sum of all or many of the s-risks.
- In phenomena with a heavy-tailed distribution, the most extreme 0.1% of cases rarely contain 99% of the total distribution. Thus, it makes sense to focus, for example, on the worst 10% of outcomes rather than on the worst 0.1%.
- Even the most severe 1% of s-risks may still occur in very diverse scenarios, with very diverse sources of suffering.
- Even if most future suffering occurs in a limited number of very specific worst-case scenarios, we may be mistaken about which scenarios these will be.
- Interventions against the worst risks may not be available, or may not be more efficient than interventions that could help across a wide range of risks.
- There may also be a positive tail in the future, which would come from the opportunity to reduce, for example, natural s-risks[69]. Thus, we should try to reduce the negative tail and increase the positive one and, for that reason, prefer interventions that cover many kinds of scenarios.
Baumann (2022, p. 39) concludes that all these observations concern what we should do as a group. Individually, it may make sense to specialize in a narrow range of risks, as long as our collective efforts cover a broad range of risks.

**Notes**

[66] One example is the position defended by Baumann (2022, p. 36-40).
[67] On why this is an s-risk, see O'brien (2022).
[68] On why this is an s-risk, see Tomasik (2015) and Baumann (2022, p. 11-16, 19, 50, 52, 58-61, 83-4).
[69] On how natural processes typically harm nonhuman animals on a large scale, see Cunha (2022) and Animal Ethics (2023[2020]).

### Identifying Risk Factors for S-Risks

https://questaodeetica.biblioverse.org/en/v9/08-identifying-risk-factors-for-s-risks.html

#### 8.1 What risk factors are and why it is important to identify them

One of the most common objections to concern for the long-term future[70] is the difficulty of estimating the long-term consequences of each decision. For example, it is hard to assess how a given intervention would affect s-risks (that is, risks of suffering of astronomical magnitude in the future[71]), since there are countless possible s-risks and the future is highly uncertain. One possible way out of this difficulty is to try to investigate *risk factors*[72], which are not themselves s-risks but greatly increase their likelihood or severity.

The concept of a *risk factor* is already widely used in medicine. For example, smoking, lack of exercise, and poor diet are not health problems in themselves, but they can lead to many diseases. To know that it is good to prevent these factors, we do not need to analyze specific diseases or know what each person's health trajectory will be. Analogously, if we discover what the risk factors for s-risks are, we do not need to know what the future will be like to know that it is good to prevent them.

As with risk factors in medicine, this does not mean that risk factors for s-risks would necessarily cause one or more s-risks to materialize. It means only that they would greatly increase their likelihood. Thus, if we identify such risk factors, we will be able to plan effective interventions to reduce a wide range of s-risks, without needing to know what the future will be like.

Baumann (2002.p. 49-56) suggests several examples of risk factors for s-risks. In the following sections we will discuss each of them separately, and in section 8.9 we will discuss the interaction among these various risk factors.

#### 8.2 Advanced technology

Many s-risks are possible only because of new technologies. However, every technological

advance is worrying to a greater or lesser degree. Among the most worrying are technologies that could make it very easy to create large amounts of suffering. Here are two examples.

- The ability to create digital sentient beings[73] could result in enormous amounts of suffering because of the disregard for nonbiological sentient beings, something we addressed in section 1.8.3.
- Space colonization could vastly multiply the population of sentient beings, who would be subject both to the decisions of agents and to natural processes[74]. There are between 100 and 400 billion stars in our galaxy, and between 100 and 200 billion galaxies in the universe[75]. Without space colonization, suffering would be limited to that on Earth (which is already enormous, but tiny compared with what could arise).
#### 8.3 Aversion to technology

Technology also offers opportunities to reduce s-risks. For example, if technological progress were halted, this would prevent the emergence of s-risks caused by humans, but it would not prevent natural s-risks (on Earth or beyond it) or those caused by other civilizations, should these exist (and it would also mean that there would be no technology to prevent these other s-risks).

Technology is a tool. As such, it will be used to achieve the ends of those who use it. Thus, whether a technology will increase or reduce suffering depends on the goals of those who will make use of it. For example, space colonization could multiply s-risks beyond Earth, but it could also make it possible to reduce s-risks, if there are s-risks beyond Earth.

Of course, it could be said that, with respect to certain technologies, such as space colonization, the risk they pose of causing s-risks is so great that it might still be worth never using them, even if this means failing to prevent suffering

as well. However, even if it had been shown that, because of this risk, it is better never to develop certain technologies, this would not support the claim that it is better to halt technological progress as a whole (since it would not apply to other technologies), much less to abandon already existing technology.

Moreover, we must take into account that much of the aversion to the use of technology stems from an unrealistically positive view of nature. For example, the prevailing belief is that, if humans stop harming wild animals, these animals will usually have at least minimally positive lives as a result of natural processes. This view is the opposite of reality. Natural processes tend to maximize the number of animals who are born to experience mostly suffering and to die prematurely. However, the romanticized view of nature is widespread, and it is one of the beliefs that contributes most to the mistaken idea that, by abandoning technology, suffering will decrease.

#### 8.4 Lack of consideration for nonhuman sentient beings

Most s-risks, as well as the little attention given to preventing s-risks, exist only because the level of moral consideration given to nonhuman sentient beings is low. We saw in section 1.6.1 that a lack of consideration for the individuals affected by decisions is enough for there to be an s-risk (agents need not aim at suffering for its own sake). The overwhelming majority of the potential victims of s-risks are nonhuman (whether nonhuman animals or possible future nonorganic sentient beings). Thus, the lack of consideration for nonhuman sentient beings is one of the main risk factors for s-risks. Moreover, besides being a risk factor itself, this lack of consideration also gives rise to another risk factor: the lack of efforts to reduce s-risks, which we will address next.

#### 8.5 Lack of efforts to reduce s-risks.

Progress in preventing s-risks is possible only if enough people care about this question. For example, future generations may come to have technology that could be used to prevent or minimize s-risks, but choose not to do so because they lack sufficient moral consideration for all sentient beings.

This does not mean that, for there to be efforts to reduce s-risks, there must necessarily be a very large number of people focusing on this. Even if few people focus on preventing s-risks, they can seek compromises with people who have other focuses (but who are not opposed to preventing s-risks) in order to implement low-cost measures to prevent them. Moreover, one can focus on trying to get people who have more resources, power, or influence to want to prevent s-risks. The positive impact of these people may be much greater than the combined positive impact of many people who have few resources, little power, or little influence.

#### 8.6 Misguided or ineffective efforts to reduce s-risks

Wanting to reduce s-risks is not enough. Efforts need to be well planned so that they are not of little effect, ineffective, or even counterproductive.

Some risks related to these possibilities are:

- If the cause of reducing s-risks becomes associated with highly controversial ideas, this may generate strong opposition to the proposal to prevent s-risks.
- The relevant decision-makers may want to prevent s-risks, but political institutions may be ineffective or there may be cooperation problems[76].
- It may also be that decision-makers fail to notice certain s-risks in their early stages and, by the time they do, it is already too late.
The question of efforts that are of little effect, ineffective, or counterproductive will be addressed in detail in Chapter 13.

#### 8.7 Polarization, conflict, and hostility

S-risks are more likely to occur if there is a high degree of hostility among future agents. Large-scale polarization leaves little room for reflection (about s-risks or anything else) and for mutual compromise. It also has the potential to result in conflicts and even wars, which increases the chances of agential s-risks.

Polarization, and how to reduce it, will be the subject of Chapter 11.

#### 8.8 Lack of security against agents who aim to cause suffering

Another risk factor is insufficient security against agents whose goal is to cause suffering. At present, some of these agents are restrained to some extent by moral norms and laws, but there are possible future scenarios in which such forms of restraint could be ineffective or insufficient (for example, in a future with powerful, autonomous AIs and/or with space colonization).

Individuals with personality traits such as psychopathy, sadism, narcissism, and Machiavellianism increase the probability that s-risks will materialize when they attain positions of power[77]. And it is not uncommon for them to be in such positions, since they usually have a strong desire for power and their personality gives them many advantages in that pursuit (and this desire and advantage are greater the more of these traits are found in the same individual). These risks are increased if such malevolent agents have access to advanced technology (which illustrates that the more risk factors are combined, the greater the chances of an s-risk materializing, a point we will discuss in the next section).

#### 8.9 Interaction among various risk factors and among various ways of preventing them

The various risk factors interact with one another. For example, polarization increases the chances of individuals with malignant traits coming to power. If this happens, they will probably obstruct efforts to prevent s-risks. Advanced technology, in turn, could multiply the harms caused by malignant agents, and so on. Just as in the medical context, catastrophes are more likely to occur if several risk factors coincide.

Analogously, a risk factor can be mitigated by a set of favorable circumstances. For example, advanced technology is much less worrying if consideration

for all sentient beings is more widespread and there are adequate efforts to prevent s-risks. Likewise, without space colonization, the suffering caused by a malignant dictator would be limited to Earth, and so on.

#### 8.10 Conclusion

In this chapter we have seen what risk factors are, as well as some examples of risk factors for s-risks. We have also seen that the probability of an s-risk materializing is greater when several risk factors coincide, and that the chances of preventing it are also greater if several forms of prevention coincide.

In the next chapter we will look at a classification of the kinds of strategies for preventing risk factors for s-risks.
